$$

$$

$$

$$
S_{k+tn} \equiv S_k + t C \pmod m. \tag{3}
$$
Taking $t = m$ gives
$$
S_{k+mn} \equiv S_k + m C \equiv S_k \pmod m, \tag{4}

For $j=1,\dots,n$ the number $l_j$ is the smallest positive integer with

$$
This is equivalent to
$$
S_{j-1+l_j} \equiv S_{j-1} \pmod m. \tag{5}
$$
For an index $i\ge 0$ define
$$
\tau(i) = \min\{\, t > i \mid S_t \equiv S_i \pmod m \,\}.
$$
Because of (4) the set is non‑empty (take $t=i+mn$), so $\tau(i)$ is well defined and $\tau(i)\le i+mn$.

$$
S_{u+n} \equiv S_u + C \equiv S_i + C \equiv S_{i+n}.
$$
Consequently $\tau(i+n)=u+n$. ∎

$$

## Solution

Let $C = a_1 + a_2 + \cdots + a_n$.  Define $S_0 = 0$ and for $k\ge 1$,
$$
S_k = \sum_{i=1}^{k} a_i .
$$
All congruences are taken modulo $m$.

**1.  Periodicity of the partial sums.**  
For any $k\ge 0$,
$$
S_{k+n}-S_k = \sum_{i=k+1}^{k+n} a_i .
$$
Because the sequence $(a_i)$ satisfies $a_{i+n}=a_i$ for all $i\ge 1$, the $n$ terms $a_{k+1},\dots ,a_{k+n}$ are a permutation of $a_1,\dots ,a_n$; therefore their sum equals $C$.  Hence
$$
S_{k+n}=S_k + C . \tag{1}
$$
Consequently,
$$
S_{k+n}\equiv S_k + C \pmod m . \tag{2}
$$
Replacing $k$ by $k+n$ repeatedly we obtain $S_{k+tn}\equiv S_k + t\,C \pmod m$ for every $t\ge 0$.  Taking $t=m$ gives
$$
S_{k+mn}\equiv S_k + mC \equiv S_k \pmod m , \tag{3}
$$
because $mC$ is a multiple of $m$.  Thus the sequence $(S_k \bmod m)$ is periodic with period $mn$:
$$
S_{i+mn}\equiv S_i \pmod m \qquad(\forall\, i\ge 0). \tag{4}
$$

**2.  Reformulating $l_j$.**  
For $j=1,\dots ,n$ the number $l_j$ is the smallest positive integer with
$$
m\mid a_j + a_{j+1} + \dots + a_{j+l_j-1}.
$$
This is equivalent to
$$
S_{j-1+l_j}\equiv S_{j-1} \pmod m . \tag{5}
$$
For an index $i\ge 0$ define
$$
\tau(i)=\min\{\,t>i\mid S_t\equiv S_i \pmod m \,\}.
$$
Because of (4) the set is non‑empty (one may take $t=i+mn$), so $\tau(i)$ is well defined and $\tau(i)\le i+mn$.  
From (5) we obtain
$$
l_j = \tau(j-1)-(j-1) \qquad(1\le j\le n).
$$
Therefore
$$
L:=\sum_{j=1}^{n} l_j = \sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\bigl(\tau(i)-i\bigr). \tag{6}
$$

**3.  How $\tau$ behaves when the index is shifted by $n$.**  
From (2) we have $S_{i+n}\equiv S_i + C$.

*Lemma 1.*  $\tau(i+n)=\tau(i)+n$ for every $i\ge 0$.

*Proof.*  Put $u=\tau(i)$.  Then $S_u\equiv S_i$ and $S_r\not\equiv S_i$ for all $r$ with $i<r<u$.  
Take any integer $s$ with $i+n < s < u+n$.  Then $s\ge n+1$, so $s-n\ge 1$ and we may apply (2) with $k=s-n$:
$$
S_s \equiv S_{s-n}+C .
$$
Since $i < s-n < u$, the definition of $u$ gives $S_{s-n}\not\equiv S_i$.  Hence
$$
S_s \not\equiv S_i + C \equiv S_{i+n}.
$$
Thus no index strictly between $i+n$ and $u+n$ can have residue equal to $S_{i+n}$.  On the other hand,
$$
S_{u+n}\equiv S_u + C \equiv S_i + C \equiv S_{i+n}.
$$
Therefore $u+n$ is the smallest integer $>i+n$ congruent to $S_{i+n}$; i.e. $\tau(i+n)=u+n$.  $\square$

Applying Lemma 1 repeatedly yields
$$
\tau(i+kn)=\tau(i)+kn \qquad(k\ge 0). \tag{7}
$$

**4.  Expressing $m\,L$ as a sum over $mn$ consecutive indices.**  
Set $P=mn$.  Consider
$$
\Sigma:=\sum_{i=0}^{P-1}\bigl(\tau(i)-i\bigr).
$$
Write each $i\in[0,P-1]$ uniquely as $i = r + kn$ with $0\le r\le n-1$ and $0\le k\le m-1$.  Using (7),
$$
\tau(r+kn)-(r+kn)=\bigl(\tau(r)+kn\bigr)-(r+kn)=\tau(r)-r .
$$
Hence
$$
\Sigma = \sum_{r=0}^{n-1}\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}\bigl(\tau(r)-r\bigr)
      = m\sum_{r=0}^{n-1}\bigl(\tau(r)-r\bigr)
      = m\,L . \tag{8}
$$

**5.  Computing $\Sigma$ via the $P$‑periodicity of residues.**  
Because of (4) the residues repeat every $P$:
$$
S_{i+P}\equiv S_i \pmod m \qquad(\forall\,i\ge 0). \tag{9}
$$
For each residue $r\in\{0,1,\dots ,m-1\}$ define
$$
A_r = \{\, i\in[0,P-1]\mid S_i\equiv r \pmod m \,\}.
$$
The sets $A_0,\dots ,A_{m-1}$ form a partition of $\{0,1,\dots ,P-1\}$.

If $A_r\neq\varnothing$, set
$$
a_r = \min A_r , \qquad b_r = \max A_r .
$$
From (9) one easily obtains the description of all indices whose residue equals $r$:
$$
\{\,i\ge 0\mid S_i\equiv r\,\} = \bigcup_{k\ge 0} (A_r + kP). \tag{10}
$$
(Indeed, if $S_j\equiv r$, write $j = qP+\rho$ with $0\le\rho<P$; then $S_\rho\equiv S_j\equiv r$, so $\rho\in A_r$ and $j\in A_r+qP$.  Conversely, every element of $A_r+kP$ has residue $r$ by (9).)

Now we determine $\tau$ on $A_r$.

*Claim.*  For a residue $r$ with $A_r\neq\varnothing$,
* (i) if $i\in A_r$ and $i<b_r$, then $\tau(i)=\min\{\,j\in A_r\mid j>i\,\}$;
* (ii) $\tau(b_r)=a_r+P$.

*Proof.*  By (10) any index with residue $r$ is of the form $x+kP$ with $x\in A_r$, $k\ge 0$.
* (i) Since $i<b_r$, there exists an element of $A_r$ larger than $i$.  Let $j$ be the smallest such element.  Then $j\le b_r\le P-1$.  All indices with $k\ge 1$ are at least $P$, hence larger than $j$.  Therefore the first occurrence of residue $r$ after $i$ is exactly $j$; i.e. $\tau(i)=j$.
* (ii) For $i=b_r$ there is no larger element inside $A_r$.  The next occurrence must come from a set $A_r+kP$ with $k\ge 1$.  The smallest element among those sets is $a_r+P$ (because $a_r$ is the smallest element of $A_r$).  Clearly $a_r+P > b_r$, so $\tau(b_r)=a_r+P$.  $\square$

Now compute the contribution of $A_r$ to $\Sigma$:
$$
T_r := \sum_{i\in A_r}\bigl(\tau(i)-i\bigr).
$$
List the elements of $A_r$ in increasing order:
$$
A_r = \{e_0 < e_1 < \dots < e_{t-1}\},\qquad t = |A_r|.
$$
Thus $e_0 = a_r$, $e_{t-1}=b_r$.  
By the claim,
$$
\tau(e_k) = e_{k+1}\;\; (0\le k\le t-2),\qquad
\tau(e_{t-1}) = a_r + P .
$$
Consequently
$$
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{k=0}^{t-2}\bigl(\tau(e_k)-e_k\bigr)
   &= \sum_{k=0}^{t-2}(e_{k+1}-e_k)=e_{t-1}-e_0,\\[2mm]
\tau(e_{t-1})-e_{t-1} &= (a_r+P)-e_{t-1}.
\end{aligned}
$$
Adding them,
$$
T_r = (e_{t-1}-e_0) + (a_r+P-e_{t-1}) = a_r+P-e_0 = P .
$$
(The calculation also works for $t=1$ if we interpret the empty sum as $0$; then $T_r = a_r+P-a_r = P$.)  
Thus **every non‑empty $A_r$ contributes exactly $P$ to $\Sigma$.**

Because the $A_r$’s partition $\{0,1,\dots ,P-1\}$, we have
$$
\Sigma = \sum_{r=0}^{m-1} T_r = P\cdot N,
$$
where $N = \#\{\,r\mid A_r\neq\varnothing\,\}$ is the number of residues that actually appear in the first $P$ terms (equivalently, appear at all).  Obviously $N\le m$, since there are only $m$ residues modulo $m$.  Hence
$$
\Sigma \le P\cdot m = (mn)\cdot m = m^{2}n . \tag{11}
$$

**6.  Conclusion.**  
From (8) and (11),
$$
m\,L = \Sigma \le m^{2}n \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad L \le m\,n .
$$
Recalling the definition of $L$, this is precisely
$$
l_1 + l_2 + \cdots + l_n \le m n ,
$$
which completes the proof. $\square$

**Solution**:

Let $a_1,a_2,\ldots$ be the given sequence of integers (divisibility is understood in $\mathbb Z$).  Set  

$$
C = a_1+a_2+\cdots +a_n .
$$

Define $S_0=0$ and for $k\ge 1$,
$$
S_k = \sum_{i=1}^{k} a_i .
$$
All congruences below are modulo $m$.

**1.  Periodicity of the partial sums.**  
For any $k\ge 0$,
$$
S_{k+n}-S_k = \sum_{i=k+1}^{k+n} a_i .
$$
Because $a_{i+n}=a_i$ for all $i\ge 1$, the $n$ numbers $a_{k+1},\dots ,a_{k+n}$ are a permutation of $a_1,\dots ,a_n$; hence their sum equals $C$.  Thus
$$
S_{k+n}=S_k + C . \tag{1}
$$
Consequently,
$$
S_{k+n}\equiv S_k + C \pmod m . \tag{2}
$$
Applying (2) repeatedly gives, for every $t\ge 0$,
$$
S_{k+tn}\equiv S_k + t\,C \pmod m . \tag{3}
$$
Taking $t=m$ and using $mC\equiv0\pmod m$ we obtain
$$
S_{k+mn}\equiv S_k \pmod m . \tag{4}
$$
Hence the sequence $(S_k\bmod m)$ is periodic with period $mn$:
$$
S_{i+mn}\equiv S_i \pmod m \qquad(\forall\,i\ge 0). \tag{5}
$$

**2.  Translating $l_j$ into a “next occurrence’’ function.**  
For $j=1,\dots ,n$ the number $l_j$ is the smallest positive integer with
$$
m \mid a_j + a_{j+1} + \dots + a_{j+l_j-1}.
$$
This is equivalent to
$$
S_{j-1+l_j}\equiv S_{j-1} \pmod m . \tag{6}
$$
For an index $i\ge 0$ define
$$
\tau(i)=\min\{\,t>i\mid S_t\equiv S_i \pmod m \,\}.
$$
Because of (4) the set is non‑empty (one may take $t=i+mn$), so $\tau(i)$ is well defined and $\tau(i)\le i+mn$.  
From (6) we obtain
$$
l_j = \tau(j-1)-(j-1) \qquad(1\le j\le n).
$$
Therefore
$$
L:=\sum_{j=1}^{n} l_j = \sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\bigl(\tau(i)-i\bigr). \tag{7}
$$

**3.  How $\tau$ behaves when the index is shifted by $n$.**  
From (2) we have $S_{i+n}\equiv S_i + C$.

*Lemma 1.*  $\tau(i+n)=\tau(i)+n$ for every $i\ge 0$.

*Proof.*  Put $u=\tau(i)$.  Then $S_u\equiv S_i$ and $S_r\not\equiv S_i$ for all $r$ with $i<r<u$.  
Take any integer $s$ with $i+n < s < u+n$.  Then $s\ge n+1$, so $s-n\ge 1$ and we may apply (2) with $k=s-n$:
$$
S_s \equiv S_{s-n}+C .
$$
Since $i < s-n < u$, the definition of $u$ gives $S_{s-n}\not\equiv S_i$.  Hence
$$
S_s \not\equiv S_i + C \equiv S_{i+n}.
$$
Thus no index strictly between $i+n$ and $u+n$ can have residue equal to $S_{i+n}$.  On the other hand,
$$
S_{u+n}\equiv S_u + C \equiv S_i + C \equiv S_{i+n}.
$$
Therefore $u+n$ is the smallest integer $>i+n$ congruent to $S_{i+n}$; i.e. $\tau(i+n)=u+n$.  $\square$

Applying Lemma 1 repeatedly yields
$$
\tau(i+kn)=\tau(i)+kn \qquad(k\ge 0). \tag{8}
$$

**4.  Expressing $m\,L$ as a sum over $mn$ consecutive indices.**  
Set $P=mn$.  Consider
$$
\Sigma:=\sum_{i=0}^{P-1}\bigl(\tau(i)-i\bigr).
$$
Write each $i\in[0,P-1]$ uniquely as $i = r + kn$ with $0\le r\le n-1$ and $0\le k\le m-1$.  Using (8),
$$
\tau(r+kn)-(r+kn)=\bigl(\tau(r)+kn\bigr)-(r+kn)=\tau(r)-r .
$$
Hence
$$
\Sigma = \sum_{r=0}^{n-1}\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}\bigl(\tau(r)-r\bigr)
      = m\sum_{r=0}^{n-1}\bigl(\tau(r)-r\bigr)
      = m\,L . \tag{9}
$$

**5.  Computing $\Sigma$ with the help of the $P$‑periodicity.**  
Because of (5) the residues repeat every $P$:
$$
S_{i+P}\equiv S_i \pmod m \qquad(\forall\,i\ge 0). \tag{10}
$$
For each residue $r\in\{0,1,\dots ,m-1\}$ define
$$
A_r = \{\, i\in[0,P-1]\mid S_i\equiv r \pmod m \,\}.
$$
The sets $A_0,\dots ,A_{m-1}$ form a partition of $\{0,1,\dots ,P-1\}$.

If $A_r\neq\varnothing$, set
$$
a_r = \min A_r , \qquad b_r = \max A_r .
$$
From (10) one easily obtains the description of all indices whose residue equals $r$:
$$
\{\,i\ge 0\mid S_i\equiv r\,\} = \bigcup_{k\ge 0} (A_r + kP). \tag{11}
$$
(Indeed, if $S_j\equiv r$, write $j = qP+\rho$ with $0\le\rho<P$; then $S_\rho\equiv S_j\equiv r$ by repeatedly subtracting $P$, so $\rho\in A_r$ and $j\in A_r+qP$.  Conversely, every element of $A_r+kP$ has residue $r$ by (10).)

Now we determine $\tau$ on $A_r$.

*Claim.*  For a residue $r$ with $A_r\neq\varnothing$,
* (i) if $i\in A_r$ and $i<b_r$, then $\tau(i)=\min\{\,j\in A_r\mid j>i\,\}$;
* (ii) $\tau(b_r)=a_r+P$.

*Proof.*  By (11) any index with residue $r$ is of the form $x+kP$ with $x\in A_r$, $k\ge 0$.
* (i) Since $i<b_r$, there exists an element of $A_r$ larger than $i$.  Let $j$ be the smallest such element.  Then $j\le b_r\le P-1$.  All indices with $k\ge 1$ are at least $P$, hence larger than $j$.  Therefore the first occurrence of residue $r$ after $i$ is exactly $j$; i.e. $\tau(i)=j$.
* (ii) For $i=b_r$ there is no larger element inside $A_r$.  The next occurrence must come from a set $A_r+kP$ with $k\ge 1$.  The smallest element among those sets is $a_r+P$ (because $a_r$ is the smallest element of $A_r$).  Clearly $a_r+P > b_r$, so $\tau(b_r)=a_r+P$.  $\square$

Now compute the contribution of $A_r$ to $\Sigma$:
$$
T_r := \sum_{i\in A_r}\bigl(\tau(i)-i\bigr).
$$
List the elements of $A_r$ in increasing order:
$$
A_r = \{e_0 < e_1 < \dots < e_{t-1}\},\qquad t = |A_r|.
$$
Thus $e_0 = a_r$, $e_{t-1}=b_r$.  
By the claim,
$$
\tau(e_k) = e_{k+1}\;\; (0\le k\le t-2),\qquad
\tau(e_{t-1}) = a_r + P .
$$
Consequently
$$
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{k=0}^{t-2}\bigl(\tau(e_k)-e_k\bigr)
   &= \sum_{k=0}^{t-2}(e_{k+1}-e_k)=e_{t-1}-e_0,\\[2mm]
\tau(e_{t-1})-e_{t-1} &= (a_r+P)-e_{t-1}.
\end{aligned}
$$
Adding them,
$$
T_r = (e_{t-1}-e_0) + (a_r+P-e_{t-1}) = a_r+P-e_0 = P .
$$
(The calculation is also valid for $t=1$ if we interpret the empty sum as $0$; then $e_{t-1}=e_0$ and $T_r = P$ as well.)  
Thus **every non‑empty $A_r$ contributes exactly $P$ to $\Sigma$.**

Because the $A_r$’s partition $\{0,1,\dots ,P-1\}$, we have
$$
\Sigma = \sum_{r=0}^{m-1} T_r = P\cdot N,
$$
where $N = \#\{\,r\mid A_r\neq\varnothing\,\}$ is the number of residues that actually appear in the first $P$ terms (equivalently, appear at all).  Obviously $N\le m$, since there are only $m$ residues modulo $m$.  Hence
$$
\Sigma \le P\cdot m = (mn)\cdot m = m^{2}n . \tag{12}
$$

**6.  Conclusion.**  
From (9) and (12),
$$
m\,L = \Sigma \le m^{2}n \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad L \le m\,n .
$$
Recalling the definition of $L$, this is exactly
$$
l_1 + l_2 + \cdots + l_n \le m n ,
$$
which completes the proof. $\square$

Substituting these into (2.13) and expanding we get

L = (6\sqrt2 - 3\sqrt3)(1-u^4) + 6u + 6u^3 - 3(1+2u^2+u^4)
      - 18(\sqrt3-\sqrt2)\,u(1-u^2).

Expanding the last term: -18(\sqrt3-\sqrt2)u + 18(\sqrt3-\sqrt2)u^3.  
Now collect the coefficients of powers of u.

\[
\begin{aligned}
L &= \bigl(6\sqrt2 - 3\sqrt3 - 3\bigr) \\
  &\quad + \bigl(6 + 18\sqrt2 - 18\sqrt3\bigr)u \\
  &\quad - 6u^2 \\
  &\quad + \bigl(6 + 18\sqrt3 - 18\sqrt2\bigr)u^3 \\
  &\quad + \bigl(-6\sqrt2 + 3\sqrt3 - 3\bigr)u^4 .
\end{aligned}
\tag{2.14}
\]

---

**Extracting a factor \(1-u\).**  
One checks that substituting u = 1 makes L vanish (this corresponds to s = 0, t = \sqrt{3/2}, a case where equality holds). Hence \(1-u\) divides L. Write

L = (1-u)\,Q(u), \qquad Q(u) = p u^3 + q u^2 + r u + s_0.

Expanding the right‑hand side,

(1-u)(p u^3 + q u^2 + r u + s_0) = -p u^4 + (p-q)u^3 + (q-r)u^2 + (r-s_0)u + s_0.

Comparing with (2.14) we obtain the system

\[
\begin{aligned}
-p &= -6\sqrt2 + 3\sqrt3 - 3,\\
p-q &= 6 + 18\sqrt3 - 18\sqrt2,\\
q-r &= -6,\\
r-s_0 &= 6 + 18\sqrt2 - 18\sqrt3,\\
s_0 &= 6\sqrt2 - 3\sqrt3 - 3 .
\end{aligned}
\]

Solving successively:

\[
\begin{aligned}
p &= 6\sqrt2 - 3\sqrt3 + 3,\\[2mm]
q &= p - (6 + 18\sqrt3 - 18\sqrt2) = 24\sqrt2 - 21\sqrt3 - 3,\\[2mm]
r &= q + 6 = 24\sqrt2 - 21\sqrt3 + 3,\\[2mm]
s_0 &= r - (6 + 18\sqrt2 - 18\sqrt3) = 6\sqrt2 - 3\sqrt3 - 3 .
\end{aligned}
\]

The last line indeed matches the constant term of L, confirming the consistency.  
Thus we have

L = (1-u)\,Q(u) \quad\text{with}\quad
Q(u) = p u^3 + q u^2 + r u + s_0, \tag{2.15}

the coefficients \(p,q,r,s_0\) being those just found.

Because \(D^2 = (1+u^2)^2 > 0\), the original inequality (2.9) is equivalent to \(L \ge 0\). Since \(u\in[0,1]\) gives \(1-u \ge 0\), it is enough to prove

Q(u) \ge 0 \qquad (0\le u\le 1). \tag{2.16}

---

**Factoring \(Q(u)\).**  
Set

u_0 = \frac{\sqrt3 - 1}{\sqrt2}\;(>0),\qquad\text{so that}\qquad u_0^2 = 2 - \sqrt3.

A direct computation shows that \(Q(u)\) possesses a double root at \(u_0\).  
Indeed, define

u_1 = -\frac{s_0}{p\,u_0^2}. \tag{2.17}

We claim that

Q(u) = p\,(u - u_0)^2\,(u - u_1). \tag{2.18}

To verify this, it suffices to check the coefficients of \(u^2\) and \(u\) because the leading coefficient and the constant term already match by the choice of \(u_1\) (indeed the constant term of the right‑hand side is \(p\,u_0^2(-u_1) = s_0\)).  

Compute the needed quantities:

\[
\begin{aligned}
p\,u_0^2 &= (6\sqrt2 - 3\sqrt3 + 3)(2-\sqrt3) \\
        &= 12\sqrt2 - 6\sqrt6 - 9\sqrt3 + 15,\\[2mm]
s_0 &= 6\sqrt2 - 3\sqrt3 - 3,\\[2mm]
u_1 &= -\frac{6\sqrt2 - 3\sqrt3 - 3}{12\sqrt2 - 6\sqrt6 - 9\sqrt3 + 15}\; (<0).
\end{aligned}
\]

Now evaluate the coefficient of \(u^2\) in (2.18):

\[
-p(2u_0 + u_1) = -2p u_0 - p u_1 = -2p u_0 + \frac{s_0}{u_0^2},
\]
because \(p u_1 = -s_0/u_0^2\).  

Compute \(-2p u_0\).  Since \(u_0 = (\sqrt3-1)/\sqrt2\),

\[
-2p u_0 = -2p\frac{\sqrt3-1}{\sqrt2} = \sqrt2\,p\,(1-\sqrt3).
\]

Now \(\sqrt2\,p = \sqrt2(6\sqrt2 - 3\sqrt3 + 3) = 12 - 3\sqrt6 + 3\sqrt2\). Multiplying by \((1-\sqrt3)\):

\[
\sqrt2\,p\,(1-\sqrt3) = (12 - 3\sqrt6 + 3\sqrt2)(1-\sqrt3)
 = 12 - 12\sqrt3 + 12\sqrt2 - 6\sqrt6 .
\]

Next, \(s_0/u_0^2 = s_0(2+\sqrt3)\) because \(1/u_0^2 = 2+\sqrt3\).  Thus

\[
\frac{s_0}{u_0^2} = (6\sqrt2 - 3\sqrt3 - 3)(2+\sqrt3)
 = 12\sqrt2 + 6\sqrt6 - 9\sqrt3 - 15 .
\]

Adding the two pieces,

\[
-p(2u_0 + u_1) = \bigl(12 - 12\sqrt3 + 12\sqrt2 - 6\sqrt6\bigr)
                + \bigl(12\sqrt2 + 6\sqrt6 - 9\sqrt3 - 15\bigr)
                = 24\sqrt2 - 21\sqrt3 - 3 = q .
\]

Hence the coefficient of \(u^2\) matches.

Now examine the coefficient of \(u\) in (2.18):

\[
p(u_0^2 + 2u_0 u_1) = p u_0^2 + 2p u_0 u_1
 = p u_0^2 - \frac{2s_0}{u_0},
\]
since \(p u_1 = -s_0/u_0^2\) gives \(2p u_0 u_1 = -2s_0/u_0\).

We already have \(p u_0^2 = 12\sqrt2 - 6\sqrt6 - 9\sqrt3 + 15\).  
Compute \(2s_0/u_0\).  Because \(1/u_0 = \frac{\sqrt2}{\sqrt3-1} = \frac{\sqrt2(\sqrt3+1)}{2}\),

\[
\frac{2s_0}{u_0} = s_0\sqrt2\,(\sqrt3+1)
 = \sqrt2(6\sqrt2 - 3\sqrt3 - 3)(\sqrt3+1).
\]

First, \(\sqrt2(6\sqrt2 - 3\sqrt3 - 3) = 12 - 3\sqrt6 - 3\sqrt2\).  Multiplying by \((\sqrt3+1)\):

\[
(12 - 3\sqrt6 - 3\sqrt2)(\sqrt3+1)
 = 12\sqrt3 + 12 - 3\sqrt{18} - 3\sqrt6 - 3\sqrt6 - 3\sqrt2
 = 12\sqrt3 + 12 - 9\sqrt2 - 6\sqrt6 - 3\sqrt2
 = 12\sqrt3 + 12 - 12\sqrt2 - 6\sqrt6 .
\]

Therefore

\[
p(u_0^2 + 2u_0 u_1) = \bigl(12\sqrt2 - 6\sqrt6 - 9\sqrt3 + 15\bigr)
                     - \bigl(12\sqrt3 + 12 - 12\sqrt2 - 6\sqrt6\bigr)
 = 24\sqrt2 - 21\sqrt3 + 3 = r .
\]

Thus the coefficient of \(u\) also coincides.  Consequently (2.18) holds.

---

**Positivity of \(Q(u)\).**  
We have \(p = 6\sqrt2 - 3\sqrt3 + 3 > 0\) (numerically \(p \approx 6.289\)).  Moreover \(s_0 > 0\) and \(u_0^2 > 0\), so \(u_1 = -s_0/(p u_0^2) < 0\).  Hence for every \(u \ge 0\),

\[
u - u_1 > 0,\qquad (u - u_0)^2 \ge 0,
\]
and consequently

\[
Q(u) = p\,(u - u_0)^2\,(u - u_1) \ge 0 .
\]

In particular \(Q(u) \ge 0\) for all \(u\in[0,1]\).

---

**Conclusion of the case \(m = \sqrt6-2\).**  
From \(L = (1-u)Q(u)\) and \(1-u \ge 0\) on \([0,1]\) we obtain \(L \ge 0\).  Since \(L = G\cdot D^2\) with \(D^2>0\), the left‑hand side \(G\) of (2.9) is non‑negative.  Thus (2.9) holds for all admissible \(s,t\).

---

**Return to the original \(m\).**  
Recall that for any \(m \in [\sqrt6-2,\,1/\sqrt3]\) the left‑hand side of (2.7) is \(L(m) = s+2t-3 + mQ\) with \(Q \ge 0\).  Because we have proved \(L(m_0) \ge 0\) for \(m_0 = \sqrt6-2\), the monotonicity in \(m\) yields \(L(m) \ge L(m_0) \ge 0\) for all \(m \ge m_0\).  Hence (2.7) is true for every \(m\) in the prescribed interval.

---

**Final step.**  
We have shown that the inequality holds whenever two variables are equal.  By the uvw argument presented at the beginning, this is sufficient to guarantee the inequality for all positive \(a,b,c\) satisfying \(a^2+b^2+c^2 = 3\).  Therefore

\[
\frac{1}{1 - m a} + \frac{1}{1 - m b} + \frac{1}{1 - m c} \ge \frac{3}{1 - m}
\qquad
\bigl(a,b,c>0,\; a^2+b^2+c^2 = 3,\; \sqrt6-2 \le m \le \tfrac{1}{\sqrt3}\bigr).
\]

This completes the proof of part (2).

## Solution  

### Part (1)  
Let \(a,b,c>0\) with \(a+b+c=3\) and \(0\le m\le \frac13\).  
Define \(f(x)=\dfrac1{1-mx}\) for \(x\in\bigl(0,\frac1m\bigr)\).  
Because \(a,b,c<3\) and \(m\le\frac13\), we have \(1-ma>0\) etc.  
\(f''(x)=\dfrac{2m^2}{(1-mx)^3}>0\); hence \(f\) is convex.  
Jensen’s inequality gives  

\[
\frac{f(a)+f(b)+f(c)}{3}\ge f\!\left(\frac{a+b+c}{3}\right)=f(1)=\frac1{1-m}.
\]

Multiplying by \(3\) yields the required inequality.  

---

### Part (2)  
Let \(a,b,c>0\) with \(a^2+b^2+c^2=3\) and  

\[
\sqrt6-2\;\le\; m\;\le\;\frac1{\sqrt3}.
\]

Then \(m>0\).  Because \(a,b,c<\sqrt3\) and \(m\le\frac1{\sqrt3}\), we have \(1-ma>0\) (and similarly for \(b,c\)); all denominators are positive.

---

#### 1.  A convenient equivalent form  

\[
\frac1{1-ma}-\frac1{1-m}= \frac{m(a-1)}{(1-m)(1-ma)},
\]

hence the desired inequality is equivalent to  

\[
\sum_{\text{cyc}}\frac{a-1}{1-ma}\ge0. \tag{1}
\]

Multiplying by the positive product \(\prod (1-ma)\) we obtain an equivalent polynomial inequality  

\[
N:=\sum_{\text{cyc}}(a-1)(1-mb)(1-mc)\ge0. \tag{2}
\]

---

#### 2.  Expressing \(N\) through symmetric sums  

Let  

\[
p=a+b+c,\qquad q=ab+bc+ca,\qquad r=abc.
\]

Expand \((1-mb)(1-mc)=1-m(b+c)+m^2bc\).  Then  

\[
\begin{aligned}
N&=\sum (a-1)-m\sum (a-1)(b+c)+m^2\sum (a-1)bc \\[2mm]
&=(p-3)-m(2q-2p)+m^2(3r-q) \\[2mm]
&=p(1+2m)-3-q(2m+m^2)+3m^2r. \tag{3}
\end{aligned}
\]

The condition \(a^2+b^2+c^2=3\) gives \(p^2-2q=3\), i.e.  

\[
q=\frac{p^2-3}{2}. \tag{4}
\]

Substituting (4) into (3) yields  

\[
N=(1+2m)p-3-(2m+m^2)\frac{p^2-3}{2}+3m^2r. \tag{5}
\]

---

#### 3.  Reducing to the case \(b=c\) (the \(uvw\) method)  

In (5) the coefficient of \(r\) is \(3m^2>0\); therefore for a fixed \(p\) (and hence fixed \(q\) by (4)) the expression \(N\) is an increasing function of \(r\).  
Consequently, to prove \(N\ge0\) for all admissible triples it suffices to prove it when \(r\) is as small as possible (for each \(p\)).  

For fixed \(p,q\) the numbers \(a,b,c\) are the roots of  

\[
t^3-pt^2+qt-r=0.
\]

The condition that the roots are real (and non‑negative) forces the discriminant to be non‑negative; the minimal possible value of \(r\) corresponds to the discriminant being zero – i.e. the cubic has a double root, which means two variables are equal. (The case where one variable is zero also gives \(r=0\) and is covered by the limit of two equal variables.)  
Hence it is enough to check the inequality when two variables are equal.  By symmetry we may assume  

\[
b=c=t\;(t\ge0),\qquad a=s\;(s>0).
\]

The constraint becomes  

\[
s^2+2t^2=3. \tag{6}
\]

Now substitute \(b=c=t,\;a=s\) directly into the original inequality.  Clearing the positive denominators \((1-mt)(1-ms)(1-m)\) we obtain the equivalent form  

\[
s+2t-3+m\bigl(2s+t-3st\bigr)\ge0. \tag{7}
\]

---

#### 4.  A useful inequality  

Set  

\[
Q:=2s+t-3st.
\]

We claim that \(Q\ge0\) for all \(s,t\ge0\) satisfying (6).  
If \(s=0\) or \(t=0\) the inequality is obvious, so assume \(s,t>0\).  

From (6) and AM–GM,  

\[
1=\frac{s^2+t^2+t^2}{3}\ge\sqrt[3]{s^2t^4}\;\Longrightarrow\;st^2\le1. \tag{8}
\]

Apply AM–GM to \(\frac1t,\frac1t,\frac1s\):

\[
\frac{\frac2t+\frac1s}{3}\ge\sqrt[3]{\frac1{t^2s}}
\;\Longrightarrow\;
\frac2t+\frac1s\ge\frac3{\sqrt[3]{t^2s}}.
\]

Because of (8), \(\sqrt[3]{t^2s}\le1\); therefore \(\frac3{\sqrt[3]{t^2s}}\ge3\).  Hence  

\[
\frac2t+\frac1s\ge3\quad\Longrightarrow\quad 2s+t\ge3st,
\]

i.e. \(Q\ge0\).  Equality holds exactly at \(s=t=1\).

---

#### 5.  Reduction to the smallest \(m\)

The left‑hand side of (7) is  

\[
L(m)=s+2t-3+mQ,
\]

and \(Q\ge0\).  Thus \(L(m)\) is non‑decreasing in \(m\).  The problem asks for the inequality for all  

\[
m\in\bigl[m_0,m_1\bigr],\qquad 
m_0=\sqrt6-2,\;\; m_1=\frac1{\sqrt3}.
\]

Consequently it suffices to prove (7) for the smallest value \(m=m_0\); larger \(m\) will then automatically satisfy it.  So we need to show  

\[
s+2t-3+(\sqrt6-2)(2s+t-3st)\ge0 \tag{9}
\]

under the condition (6).

---

#### 6.  A rational parametrisation of the ellipse  

The relation \(s^2+2t^2=3\) can be parametrised by  

\[
s=\sqrt3\,\frac{1-u^2}{1+u^2},\qquad 
t=\frac{\sqrt6\;u}{1+u^2},\qquad u\in[0,1]. \tag{10}
\]

(Indeed, substituting gives \(s^2+2t^2=3\).)  
For \(u=0\) we have \((s,t)=(\sqrt3,0)\); for \(u=1\) we have \((s,t)=(0,\sqrt{3/2})\).  

Insert (10) into (9).  Denote  

\[
D=1+u^2,\qquad k=\sqrt6-2.
\]

Then  

\[
\begin{aligned}
s+2t &=\frac{\sqrt3(1-u^2)+2\sqrt6\,u}{D},\\[1mm]
2s+t &=\frac{2\sqrt3(1-u^2)+\sqrt6\,u}{D},\\[1mm]
3st &=\frac{9\sqrt2\,u(1-u^2)}{D^2}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Let \(G\) be the left‑hand side of (9).  Multiplying by \(D^2>0\) we obtain  

\[
\begin{aligned}
L&:=G\cdot D^2 \\
&=\bigl(\sqrt3(1-u^2)+2\sqrt6\,u\bigr)D-3D^2
   +k\Bigl[\bigl(2\sqrt3(1-u^2)+\sqrt6\,u\bigr)D-9\sqrt2\,u(1-u^2)\Bigr]. \tag{11}
\end{aligned}
\]

A convenient simplification is to combine the two brackets that are multiplied by \(D\).  Notice that  

\[
\begin{aligned}
&\sqrt3(1-u^2)+2\sqrt6\,u \;+\; k\bigl(2\sqrt3(1-u^2)+\sqrt6\,u\bigr)\\
&\qquad = (6\sqrt2-3\sqrt3)(1-u^2)+6u. \tag{12}
\end{aligned}
\]

(Indeed, \(k\cdot2\sqrt3 = 6\sqrt2-4\sqrt3\) and \(k\cdot\sqrt6 = 6-2\sqrt6\); adding the first part gives the right‑hand side.)  

Using (12) in (11) gives  

\[
L = \bigl[(6\sqrt2-3\sqrt3)(1-u^2)+6u\bigr]D-3D^2-9k\sqrt2\,u(1-u^2). \tag{13}
\]

Now \(D=1+u^2\), hence  

\[
\bigl[(6\sqrt2-3\sqrt3)(1-u^2)+6u\bigr]D
= (6\sqrt2-3\sqrt3)(1-u^4)+6u(1+u^2).
\]

Also \(9k\sqrt2 = 9(\sqrt6-2)\sqrt2 = 18(\sqrt3-\sqrt2)\).  Substituting these into (13) and expanding:

\[
\begin{aligned}
L =& (6\sqrt2-3\sqrt3)(1-u^4)+6u+6u^3 \\
   &-3(1+2u^2+u^4)-18(\sqrt3-\sqrt2)u(1-u^2).
\end{aligned}
\]

Expanding the last term: \(-18(\sqrt3-\sqrt2)u+18(\sqrt3-\sqrt2)u^3\).  Collecting coefficients of powers of \(u\) we obtain  

\[
\begin{aligned}
L =&\bigl(6\sqrt2-3\sqrt3-3\bigr) \\
   &+\bigl(6+18\sqrt2-18\sqrt3\bigr)u \\
   &-6u^2 \\
   &+\bigl(6+18\sqrt3-18\sqrt2\bigr)u^3 \\
   &+\bigl(-6\sqrt2+3\sqrt3-3\bigr)u^4 . \tag{14}
\end{aligned}
\]

---

#### 7.  Factoring out \(1-u\)  

One checks that \(L(1)=0\) (this corresponds to \(s=0,\;t=\sqrt{3/2}\), an equality case).  Hence \(1-u\) divides \(L\).  Write  

\[
L = (1-u)\,Q(u),\qquad Q(u)=p u^3+q u^2+r u+s_0.
\]

Expanding the right‑hand side:

\[
(1-u)Q(u) = -p u^4+(p-q)u^3+(q-r)u^2+(r-s_0)u+s_0.
\]

Comparing with (14) we obtain the system  

\[
\begin{aligned}
-p &= -6\sqrt2+3\sqrt3-3,\\
p-q &= 6+18\sqrt3-18\sqrt2,\\
q-r &= -6,\\
r-s_0 &= 6+18\sqrt2-18\sqrt3,\\
s_0 &= 6\sqrt2-3\sqrt3-3 .
\end{aligned}
\]

Solving successively:

\[
\begin{aligned}
p &= 6\sqrt2-3\sqrt3+3,\\[1mm]
q &= p-(6+18\sqrt3-18\sqrt2)=24\sqrt2-21\sqrt3-3,\\[1mm]
r &= q+6 = 24\sqrt2-21\sqrt3+3,\\[1mm]
s_0 &= r-(6+18\sqrt2-18\sqrt3)=6\sqrt2-3\sqrt3-3 .
\end{aligned}
\]

The last line indeed matches the constant term of \(L\); thus the factorisation is consistent.  Consequently  

\[
L = (1-u)\,Q(u),\qquad 
Q(u)=p u^3+q u^2+r u+s_0, \tag{15}
\]

with the coefficients above.  

Because \(D^2>0\), the original inequality (9) is equivalent to \(L\ge0\).  For \(u\in[0,1]\) we have \(1-u\ge0\); therefore it is enough to prove  

\[
Q(u)\ge0\qquad(0\le u\le1). \tag{16}
\]

---

#### 8.  Factoring \(Q(u)\)  

Set  

\[
u_0=\frac{\sqrt3-1}{\sqrt2}\;(>0),\qquad\text{so that}\qquad u_0^2=2-\sqrt3.
\]

We claim that \(Q(u)\) has a double root at \(u_0\).  Define  

\[
u_1 = -\frac{s_0}{p\,u_0^2}. \tag{17}
\]

We shall verify that  

\[
Q(u)=p\,(u-u_0)^2\,(u-u_1). \tag{18}
\]

The leading coefficient and the constant term already match because the constant term of the right‑hand side is \(p\,u_0^2(-u_1)=s_0\).  It remains to check the coefficients of \(u^2\) and \(u\).

First compute  

\[
\begin{aligned}
p\,u_0^2 &= (6\sqrt2-3\sqrt3+3)(2-\sqrt3) \\
        &= 12\sqrt2-6\sqrt6-9\sqrt3+15,\\[2mm]
s_0 &= 6\sqrt2-3\sqrt3-3,\\[2mm]
u_1 &= -\frac{6\sqrt2-3\sqrt3-3}{12\sqrt2-6\sqrt6-9\sqrt3+15}\;( <0).
\end{aligned}
\]

---

**Coefficient of \(u^2\).**  In (18) it equals \(-p(2u_0+u_1)\).  Using \(p u_1 = -s_0/u_0^2\),

\[
-p(2u_0+u_1) = -2p u_0 + \frac{s_0}{u_0^2}.
\]

Now  

\[
-2p u_0 = -2p\frac{\sqrt3-1}{\sqrt2}= \sqrt2\,p\,(1-\sqrt3).
\]

\[
\sqrt2\,p = \sqrt2(6\sqrt2-3\sqrt3+3)=12-3\sqrt6+3\sqrt2,
\]
\[
\sqrt2\,p\,(1-\sqrt3)= (12-3\sqrt6+3\sqrt2)(1-\sqrt3)
=12-12\sqrt3+12\sqrt2-6\sqrt6.
\]

Next, \(s_0/u_0^2 = s_0(2+\sqrt3)\) (because \(1/u_0^2=2+\sqrt3\)):

\[
\frac{s_0}{u_0^2}= (6\sqrt2-3\sqrt3-3)(2+\sqrt3)
=12\sqrt2+6\sqrt6-9\sqrt3-15.
\]

Adding the two pieces:

\[
-p(2u_0+u_1)= \bigl(12-12\sqrt3+12\sqrt2-6\sqrt6\bigr)
              +\bigl(12\sqrt2+6\sqrt6-9\sqrt3-15\bigr)
            = 24\sqrt2-21\sqrt3-3 = q .
\]

Thus the \(u^2\) coefficient matches.

---

**Coefficient of \(u\).**  In (18) it equals \(p(u_0^2+2u_0 u_1)\).  Using \(p u_1 = -s_0/u_0^2\),

\[
p(u_0^2+2u_0 u_1)=p u_0^2 + 2p u_0 u_1 = p u_0^2 - \frac{2s_0}{u_0}.
\]

We already have \(p u_0^2 = 12\sqrt2-6\sqrt6-9\sqrt3+15\).  

Now \(2s_0/u_0\).  Since \(1/u_0 = \frac{\sqrt2}{\sqrt3-1}= \frac{\sqrt2(\sqrt3+1)}{2}\),

\[
\frac{2s_0}{u_0}= s_0\sqrt2\,(\sqrt3+1).
\]

\[
\sqrt2\,s_0 = \sqrt2(6\sqrt2-3\sqrt3-3)=12-3\sqrt6-3\sqrt2,
\]
\[
\sqrt2\,s_0(\sqrt3+1)= (12-3\sqrt6-3\sqrt2)(\sqrt3+1)
=12\sqrt3+12-9\sqrt2-6\sqrt6-3\sqrt2
=12\sqrt3+12-12\sqrt2-6\sqrt6.
\]

Therefore  

\[
p(u_0^2+2u_0 u_1)= \bigl(12\sqrt2-6\sqrt6-9\sqrt3+15\bigr)
                  -\bigl(12\sqrt3+12-12\sqrt2-6\sqrt6\bigr)
                = 24\sqrt2-21\sqrt3+3 = r .
\]

So the \(u\) coefficient also matches.  Hence (18) is proved.

---

#### 9.  Positivity of \(Q(u)\)

### (1)  
Let  

\[
S=a+b+c+d,\qquad P=abc+abd+acd+bcd,\qquad Q=abcd .
\]

---
**Lemma.**  
\[
(a+b)(b+c)(c+d)(d+a)=SP+(ac-bd)^2 .
\]

*Proof.*  Put \(X=ac+bd\).  Then  

\[
\begin{aligned}
(a+b)(c+d) &= ac+ad+bc+bd = X+ad+bc,\\
(b+c)(d+a) &= bd+ab+cd+ac = X+ab+cd .
\end{aligned}
\]

Hence  

\[
\begin{aligned}
(a+b)(b+c)(c+d)(d+a) &= (X+ad+bc)(X+ab+cd)  \\
&= X^{2}+X(ad+bc+ab+cd)+(ad+bc)(ab+cd).
\end{aligned}
\]

Now expand the second part:

\[
\begin{aligned}
X(ad+bc+ab+cd) &= (ac+bd)(ad+bc+ab+cd)  \\
&= a^{2}cd+abc^{2}+a^{2}bc+ac^{2}d+abd^{2}+b^{2}cd+ab^{2}d+bcd^{2},\\[2mm]
(ad+bc)(ab+cd) &= a^{2}bd+acd^{2}+ab^{2}c+bc^{2}d .
\end{aligned}
\]

Adding these twelve terms we obtain exactly the sum \(\displaystyle\sum_{\text{sym}}a^{2}bc\) (every monomial of the form \(x^{2}yz\) with distinct \(x,y,z\) appears once).  Therefore  

\[
(a+b)(b+c)(c+d)(d+a)=X^{2}+\sum_{\text{sym}}a^{2}bc .\tag{1}
\]

On the other hand  

\[

### 1.

Let us define vectors in $\mathbb{R}^2$ as

\[
\mathbf{u} = (x,0),\qquad 
\mathbf{v} = \Bigl(-\frac{y}{2},\ \frac{\sqrt3}{2}\,y\Bigr),\qquad 
\mathbf{w} = \Bigl(-\frac{z}{2},\ -\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\,z\Bigr).
\]

Then $|\mathbf{u}| = x$, $|\mathbf{v}| = y$, $|\mathbf{w}| = z$. Their scalar products are

\[
\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}= -\frac{xy}{2},\qquad 
\mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{w}= -\frac{yz}{2},\qquad 
\mathbf{w}\cdot\mathbf{u}= -\frac{zx}{2}.
\]

Now compute

\[
\begin{aligned}
|\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}|^{2} &= |\mathbf{u}|^{2}+|\mathbf{v}|^{2}+2\mathbf{u}\!\cdot\!\mathbf{v}
= x^{2}+y^{2}-xy,\\[2mm]
|\mathbf{v}+\mathbf{w}|^{2} &= y^{2}+z^{2}-yz,\\[2mm]
|\mathbf{w}+\mathbf{u}|^{2} &= z^{2}+x^{2}-zx,\\[2mm]
|\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}+\mathbf{w}|^{2} &= x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}+2(\mathbf{u}\!\cdot\!\mathbf{v}+\mathbf{v}\!\cdot\!\mathbf{w}+\mathbf{w}\!\cdot\!\mathbf{u})\\
&= x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}-(xy+yz+zx).
\end{aligned}
\]

Hence

\[
|\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}| = \sqrt{x^{2}-xy+y^{2}},\quad
|\mathbf{v}+\mathbf{w}| = \sqrt{y^{2}-yz+z^{2}},\quad
|\mathbf{w}+\mathbf{u}| = \sqrt{z^{2}-zx+x^{2}},
\]
\[
|\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}+\mathbf{w}| = \sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}-xy-yz-zx}.
\]

Therefore the required inequality becomes

\[
|\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}|+|\mathbf{v}+\mathbf{w}|+|\mathbf{w}+\mathbf{u}|
\le |\mathbf{u}|+|\mathbf{v}|+|\mathbf{w}|+|\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}+\mathbf{w}|. \tag{1}
\]

Inequality (1) is exactly **Hlawka’s inequality** for three vectors in an inner‑product space.  
We prove it in full generality.

> **Hlawka’s inequality.** For any vectors $\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b},\mathbf{c}$ in an inner‑product space,
> \[
> |\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}|+|\mathbf{b}+\mathbf{c}|+|\mathbf{c}+\mathbf{a}|
> \le |\mathbf{a}|+|\mathbf{b}|+|\mathbf{c}|+|\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}+\mathbf{c}|.
> \]

*Proof.*  Set  

\[
S = |\mathbf{a}|+|\mathbf{b}|+|\mathbf{c}|,\qquad 
P = |\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}|+|\mathbf{b}+\mathbf{c}|+|\mathbf{c}+\mathbf{a}|,\qquad 
T = |\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}+\mathbf{c}|.
\]

If $S=T=0$ then all vectors are $\mathbf{0}$ and the inequality is trivial.  
Thus we may assume $S+T>0$.

For any two vectors $\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}$ we have  

\[
(|\mathbf{x}|+|\mathbf{y}|)^{2}-|\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{y}|^{2}
=2\bigl(|\mathbf{x}||\mathbf{y}|-\mathbf{x}\!\cdot\!\mathbf{y}\bigr). \tag{2}
\]

Consequently, whenever $|\mathbf{x}|+|\mathbf{y}|+|\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{y}|>0$,

\[
|\mathbf{x}|+|\mathbf{y}|-|\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{y}|
= \frac{2\bigl(|\mathbf{x}||\mathbf{y}|-\mathbf{x}\!\cdot\!\mathbf{y}\bigr)}
{|\mathbf{x}|+|\mathbf{y}|+|\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{y}|}. \tag{3}
\]

If the denominator vanishes then $\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{0}$ and both sides of (3) are $0$; therefore (3) can be used in all cases with the understanding that the fraction equals $0$ when its denominator is $0$.

Apply (3) to the three pairs $(\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b})$, $(\mathbf{b},\mathbf{c})$, $(\mathbf{c},\mathbf{a})$ and denote

B = |\mathbf{b}|+|\mathbf{c}|+|\mathbf{b}+\mathbf{c}|,\quad
C = |\mathbf{c}|+|\mathbf{a}|+|\mathbf{c}+\mathbf{a}|.
\]

Now compute $S^{2}-T^{2}$:

\[
\begin{aligned}
S^{2}-T^{2}
&= (|\mathbf{a}|+|\mathbf{b}|+|\mathbf{c}|)^{2}-|\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}+\mathbf{c}|^{2} \\
&= 2\Bigl(|\mathbf{a}||\mathbf{b}|-\mathbf{a}\!\cdot\!\mathbf{b}
          +|\mathbf{b}||\mathbf{c}|-\mathbf{b}\!\cdot\!\mathbf{c}
          +|\mathbf{c}||\mathbf{a}|-\mathbf{c}\!\cdot\!\mathbf{a}\Bigr). \tag{4}
\end{aligned}
\]

Hence  

\[
S-T = \frac{S^{2}-T^{2}}{S+T}

\]

**Lemma 1.** $S \le 4$.

$f$ is continuous, so it attains a maximum on $D$.

If the maximum occurs at an interior point (all coordinates $>0$), then by Lagrange multipliers there exists $\lambda$ such that  

\[
\frac{\partial f}{\partial a}=2ab+c^{2}= \lambda,\qquad
\frac{\partial f}{\partial b}=a^{2}+2bc= \lambda,\qquad
\frac{\partial f}{\partial c}=b^{2}+2ca= \lambda. \tag{8}
\]

From the first two equalities we obtain  

\[
2ab+c^{2}=a^{2}+2bc\;\Longrightarrow\; 2ab-a^{2}=2bc-c^{2}
\;\Longrightarrow\; a(2b-a)=c(2b-c). \tag{9}
\]

From the second and third equalities,  

\[
a^{2}+2bc = b^{2}+2ca\;\Longrightarrow\; a^{2}-b^{2}=2c(a-b)
\;\Longrightarrow\; (a-b)(a+b-2c)=0. \tag{10}
\]

If $a\neq b$, then $a+b=2c$.  Substitute $c=\dfrac{a+b}{2}$ into (9):

\[
a(2b-a) = \frac{a+b}{2}\Bigl(2b-\frac{a+b}{2}\Bigr)

\]

Multiplying by $4$ and expanding gives  

\[
4a(2b-a) = (a+b)(3b-a)
\;\Longrightarrow\; 8ab-4a^{2}=2ab-a^{2}+3b^{2}
\;\Longrightarrow\; 6ab-3a^{2}-3b^{2}=0,
\]

i.e. $2ab-a^{2}-b^{2}=0$, which is $-(a-b)^{2}=0$, so $a=b$, contradicting $a\neq b$.  Hence $a=b$.

Now with $a=b$, the second and third equations in (8) become  

\[
a^{2}+2ac = \lambda,\qquad a^{2}+2ca = \lambda,
\]

so they are identical.  Using the first and the third:

\[
2a^{2}+c^{2}= \lambda = a^{2}+2ca
\;\Longrightarrow\; a^{2}-2ca+c^{2}=0
\;\Longrightarrow\; (a-c)^{2}=0,
\]

hence $a=c$.  Consequently $a=b=c$.  Thus the only possible interior critical point is $a=b=c=1$, where $f=3$.

If the maximum lies on the boundary of $D$, then at least one variable equals $0$.  Because $f$ is cyclically symmetric, we may assume $c=0$ (the other cases are similar).  Then $a+b=3$ and  

\[
f = a^{2}b.
\]

\[

\[

\[

\]

Now $(c-a)^{2}=(a-c)^{2}$.  Because $a\ge b\ge c$, we have $a-c=(a-b)+(b-c)$, whence  

\[
(a-c)^{2}\ge (a-b)^{2}+(b-c)^{2},
\]
and also $a+c-b\ge0$.  Consequently  

\[
(c-a)^{2}(c+a-b) \ge \bigl[(a-b)^{2}+(b-c)^{2}\bigr](a+c-b).
\]

Insert this estimate into the right‑hand side of (11):

\[
\begin{aligned}
2\bigl(\cdots\bigr) &\ge (a-b)^{2}(a+b-c)+(b-c)^{2}(b+c-a)
                     +\bigl[(a-b)^{2}+(b-c)^{2}\bigr](a+c-b)\\
&= (a-b)^{2}\bigl[(a+b-c)+(a+c-b)\bigr]
   +(b-c)^{2}\bigl[(b+c-a)+(a+c-b)\bigr]\\
&= (a-b)^{2}\cdot2a + (b-c)^{2}\cdot2c \;\ge\; 0.
\end{aligned}
\]

Thus the left‑hand side of (11) is non‑negative, which proves the inequality. $\square$

      +2(\mathbf{u}\!\cdot\!\mathbf{v}+\mathbf{v}\!\cdot\!\mathbf{w}+\mathbf{w}\!\cdot\!\mathbf{u})\\
      &= x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}-(xy+yz+zx).
\end{aligned}
\]

Consequently  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\|\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}\| &= \sqrt{x^{2}-xy+y^{2}},\\
\|\mathbf{v}+\mathbf{w}\| &= \sqrt{y^{2}-yz+z^{2}},\\
\|\mathbf{w}+\mathbf{u}\| &= \sqrt{z^{2}-zx+x^{2}},\\
\|\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}+\mathbf{w}\| &= \sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}-xy-yz-zx}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Thus the required inequality becomes  

\[
\|\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}\|+\|\mathbf{v}+\mathbf{w}\|+\|\mathbf{w}+\mathbf{u}\|
\le \|\mathbf{u}\|+\|\mathbf{v}\|+\|\mathbf{w}\|+\|\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}+\mathbf{w}\|. \tag{1}
\]

Inequality (1) is exactly **Hlawka’s inequality** for three vectors.  
We prove it in full generality.

> **Hlawka’s inequality.** For any vectors $\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b},\mathbf{c}$ in an inner‑product space,
> \[
> \|\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}\|+\|\mathbf{b}+\mathbf{c}\|+\|\mathbf{c}+\mathbf{a}\|
> \le \|\mathbf{a}\|+\|\mathbf{b}\|+\|\mathbf{c}\|+\|\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}+\mathbf{c}\|.
> \]

*Proof.*  Denote  

\[
S = \|\mathbf{a}\|+\|\mathbf{b}\|+\|\mathbf{c}\|,\qquad
P = \|\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}\|+\|\mathbf{b}+\mathbf{c}\|+\|\mathbf{c}+\mathbf{a}\|,\qquad
T = \|\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}+\mathbf{c}\|.
\]

If $S=T=0$ then all vectors are $\mathbf{0}$ and the inequality is trivial; therefore we assume $S+T>0$.

For any two vectors $\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}$ we have  

\[
(\|\mathbf{x}\|+\|\mathbf{y}\|)^{2}-\|\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{y}\|^{2}
   = 2\bigl(\|\mathbf{x}\|\|\mathbf{y}\|-\mathbf{x}\!\cdot\!\mathbf{y}\bigr). \tag{2}
\]

The left‑hand side factors as  

\[
(\|\mathbf{x}\|+\|\mathbf{y}\|-\|\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{y}\|)
(\|\mathbf{x}\|+\|\mathbf{y}\|+\|\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{y}\|).
\]

Set $A_{\mathbf{x}\mathbf{y}} = \|\mathbf{x}\|+\|\mathbf{y}\|+\|\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{y}\|$; then  

\[
(\|\mathbf{x}\|+\|\mathbf{y}\|-\|\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{y}\|)\,A_{\mathbf{x}\mathbf{y}}
   = 2\bigl(\|\mathbf{x}\|\|\mathbf{y}\|-\mathbf{x}\!\cdot\!\mathbf{y}\bigr). \tag{3}
\]

Apply this to the three pairs $(\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b}),(\mathbf{b},\mathbf{c}),(\mathbf{c},\mathbf{a})$ and write  

\[
A = A_{\mathbf{a}\mathbf{b}},\qquad B = A_{\mathbf{b}\mathbf{c}},\qquad C = A_{\mathbf{c}\mathbf{a}}.
\]

From the triangle inequality,

\[
\|\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}\| = \|(\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}+\mathbf{c})-\mathbf{c}\|
                        \le \|\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}+\mathbf{c}\| + \|\mathbf{c}\|,
\]

hence  

\[
A = \|\mathbf{a}\|+\|\mathbf{b}\|+\|\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}\|
   \le \|\mathbf{a}\|+\|\mathbf{b}\|+\|\mathbf{c}\|+\|\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}+\mathbf{c}\|
   = S+T.
\]

The same estimate gives $B\le S+T$ and $C\le S+T$.

Now consider the pair $(\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b})$.  
If $A=0$, then $\mathbf{a}=\mathbf{b}=\mathbf{0}$; consequently $\|\mathbf{a}\|+\|\mathbf{b}\|-\|\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}\|=0$ and $\|\mathbf{a}\|\|\mathbf{b}\|-\mathbf{a}\!\cdot\!\mathbf{b}=0$, so the inequality  

\[
\|\mathbf{a}\|+\|\mathbf{b}\|-\|\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}\|
   \ge \frac{2\bigl(\|\mathbf{a}\|\|\mathbf{b}\|-\mathbf{a}\!\cdot\!\mathbf{b}\bigr)}{S+T} \tag{4}
\]

holds trivially (both sides are $0$).  
If $A>0$, then from (3)

\[
\|\mathbf{a}\|+\|\mathbf{b}\|-\|\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}\|
   = \frac{2\bigl(\|\mathbf{a}\|\|\mathbf{b}\|-\mathbf{a}\!\cdot\!\mathbf{b}\bigr)}{A}.
\]

Because $A\le S+T$ and $\|\mathbf{a}\|\|\mathbf{b}\|-\mathbf{a}\!\cdot\!\mathbf{b}\ge0$, we obtain  

\[
\frac{2\bigl(\|\mathbf{a}\|\|\mathbf{b}\|-\mathbf{a}\!\cdot\!\mathbf{b}\bigr)}{A}
   \ge \frac{2\bigl(\|\mathbf{a}\|\|\mathbf{b}\|-\mathbf{a}\!\cdot\!\mathbf{b}\bigr)}{S+T},
\]

which is exactly (4).  The same reasoning yields analogous inequalities for the pairs $(\mathbf{b},\mathbf{c})$ and $(\mathbf{c},\mathbf{a})$.  Adding the three inequalities of type (4) gives  

\[
\sum_{\text{cyc}}\bigl(\|\mathbf{a}\|+\|\mathbf{b}\|-\|\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}\|\bigr)
   \ge \frac{2\sum_{\text{cyc}}\bigl(\|\mathbf{a}\|\|\mathbf{b}\|-\mathbf{a}\!\cdot\!\mathbf{b}\bigr)}{S+T}. \tag{5}
\]

(The cyclic sum runs over $(\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b}),(\mathbf{b},\mathbf{c}),(\mathbf{c},\mathbf{a})$.)

Next compute $S^{2}-T^{2}$:

\[
\begin{aligned}
S^{2}-T^{2}
&= (\|\mathbf{a}\|+\|\mathbf{b}\|+\|\mathbf{c}\|)^{2}
   - \|\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}+\mathbf{c}\|^{2} \\
&= 2\Bigl(\|\mathbf{a}\|\|\mathbf{b}\|-\mathbf{a}\!\cdot\!\mathbf{b}
          +\|\mathbf{b}\|\|\mathbf{c}\|-\mathbf{b}\!\cdot\!\mathbf{c}
          +\|\mathbf{c}\|\|\mathbf{a}\|-\mathbf{c}\!\cdot\!\mathbf{a}\Bigr). \tag{6}
\end{aligned}
\]

Since $S+T>0$, we can write  

\[
S-T = \frac{S^{2}-T^{2}}{S+T}
     = \frac{2\sum_{\text{cyc}}\bigl(\|\mathbf{a}\|\|\mathbf{b}\|-\mathbf{a}\!\cdot\!\mathbf{b}\bigr)}{S+T}. \tag{7}
\]

Combining (5) and (7) we obtain  

\[
\sum_{\text{cyc}}\bigl(\|\mathbf{a}\|+\|\mathbf{b}\|-\|\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}\|\bigr) \ge S-T.
\]

The left‑hand side equals  

\[
\bigl(\|\mathbf{a}\|+\|\mathbf{b}\|\bigr)+\bigl(\|\mathbf{b}\|+\|\mathbf{c}\|\bigr)+\bigl(\|\mathbf{c}\|+\|\mathbf{a}\|\bigr) - P
   = 2S-P.
\]

Hence $2S-P \ge S-T$, i.e. $P \le S+T$, which is exactly Hlawka’s inequality. $\square$

Applying the proved inequality to the vectors $\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v},\mathbf{w}$ gives (1), and therefore  

\[
\sqrt{x^{2}-xy+y^{2}}+\sqrt{y^{2}-yz+z^{2}}+\sqrt{z^{2}-zx+x^{2}}
\le x+y+z+\sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}-xy-yz-zx},
\]

which completes the proof of part (1).

### 2. Second inequality  

Let $a,b,c\ge 0$ with $a+b+c=3$.  Set  

\[
p = a+b+c = 3,\qquad
q = ab+bc+ca,\qquad
r = abc.
\]

Introduce the two cyclic sums  

\[
S = a^{2}b + b^{2}c + c^{2}a,\qquad
U = a b^{2} + b c^{2} + c a^{2}.
\]

First expand the product:

\[
\begin{aligned}
P &:= (1+a^{2}b)(1+b^{2}c)(1+c^{2}a) \\
  &= 1 + (a^{2}b+b^{2}c+c^{2}a) \\
  &\quad + \bigl(a^{2}b\cdot b^{2}c + b^{2}c\cdot c^{2}a + c^{2}a\cdot a^{2}b\bigr)
     + (a^{2}b)(b^{2}c)(c^{2}a)\\[2mm]
  &= 1 + S + \bigl(a^{2}b^{3}c + b^{2}c^{3}a + c^{2}a^{3}b\bigr) + (abc)^{3}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Notice that  

\[
a^{2}b^{3}c = abc\cdot a b^{2},\quad
b^{2}c^{3}a = abc\cdot b c^{2},\quad
c^{2}a^{3}b = abc\cdot c a^{2}.
\]

Hence  

\[
a^{2}b^{3}c + b^{2}c^{3}a + c^{2}a^{3}b = r\,U,
\]

and therefore  

\[
P = 1 + S + rU + r^{3}. \tag{8}
\]

**Lemma 1.** $S \le 4$.

*Proof.*  Consider the function $f(a,b,c)=a^{2}b+b^{2}c+c^{2}a$ on the compact set  

\[
D = \{\, (a,b,c)\in\mathbb{R}^{3}\mid a,b,c\ge 0,\ a+b+c=3 \,\}.
\]

$f$ is continuous, so it attains a maximum on $D$.

If the maximum occurs at an interior point (all coordinates $>0$), then by Lagrange multipliers there exists $\lambda$ such that  

\[
\frac{\partial f}{\partial a}=2ab+c^{2}= \lambda,\qquad
\frac{\partial f}{\partial b}=a^{2}+2bc= \lambda,\qquad
\frac{\partial f}{\partial c}=b^{2}+2ca= \lambda. \tag{9}
\]

From the first two equalities,

\[
2ab+c^{2}=a^{2}+2bc \;\Longrightarrow\; 2ab-a^{2}=2bc-c^{2}
\;\Longrightarrow\; a(2b-a)=c(2b-c). \tag{10}
\]

From the second and third equalities,

\[
a^{2}+2bc = b^{2}+2ca \;\Longrightarrow\; a^{2}-b^{2}=2c(a-b)
\;\Longrightarrow\; (a-b)(a+b-2c)=0. \tag{11}
\]

If $a\neq b$, then $a+b=2c$.  Substitute $c=\dfrac{a+b}{2}$ into (10):

\[
a(2b-a) = \frac{a+b}{2}\Bigl(2b-\frac{a+b}{2}\Bigr)
        = \frac{(a+b)(3b-a)}{4}.
\]

Multiplying by $4$ and expanding gives  

\[
4a(2b-a) = (a+b)(3b-a)
\;\Longrightarrow\; 8ab-4a^{2}=2ab-a^{2}+3b^{2}
\;\Longrightarrow\; 6ab-3a^{2}-3b^{2}=0,
\]

i.e. $2ab-a^{2}-b^{2}=0$, which is $-(a-b)^{2}=0$; hence $a=b$, contradicting $a\neq b$.  Thus $a=b$.

Now with $a=b$, the first and third equations in (9) become  

\[
2a^{2}+c^{2}= \lambda,\qquad a^{2}+2ca = \lambda.
\]

Equating them yields $2a^{2}+c^{2}=a^{2}+2ca$, i.e. $a^{2}-2ca+c^{2}=0$, so $(a-c)^{2}=0$ and $a=c$.  Consequently $a=b=c$.

Thus the only possible interior critical point is $a=b=c=1$, where $f=3$.

If the maximum lies on the boundary of $D$, then at least one variable equals $0$.  The function $f$ is invariant under cyclic permutations of $(a,b,c)$; therefore we may assume $c=0$ (otherwise rotate the triple).  Then $a+b=3$ and  

\[
f = a^{2}b.
\]

By the AM–GM inequality,

\[
a^{2}b = 4\cdot\frac{a}{2}\cdot\frac{a}{2}\cdot b
       \le 4\Bigl(\frac{\frac{a}{2}+\frac{a}{2}+b}{3}\Bigr)^{\!3}
       = 4\Bigl(\frac{a+b}{3}\Bigr)^{\!3}
       = 4\cdot 1^{3}=4.
\]

Equality holds when $\dfrac{a}{2}=b$, i.e. $a=2,\ b=1$.  Hence on the boundary $f\le 4$.

Comparing the interior candidate ($3$) with the boundary maximum ($4$) we conclude that the global maximum of $f$ on $D$ is $4$.  Therefore $S=f(a,b,c)\le 4$ for all $(a,b,c)\in D$.  $\square$

**Lemma 2 (Schur’s inequality).** For $a,b,c\ge 0$,

\[
a^{3}+b^{3}+c^{3}+3abc \ge \sum_{\text{sym}}a^{2}b,
\]

where $\displaystyle\sum_{\text{sym}}a^{2}b = a^{2}b+a^{2}c+b^{2}a+b^{2}c+c^{2}a+c^{2}b$.

*Proof.*  The inequality is symmetric, so we may assume $a\ge b\ge c\ge 0$.  One can verify the identity  

\[
2\bigl(a^{3}+b^{3}+c^{3}+3abc-\sum_{\text{sym}}a^{2}b\bigr)
= (a-b)^{2}(a+b-c)+(b-c)^{2}(b+c-a)+(c-a)^{2}(c+a-b). \tag{12}
\]

Now $(c-a)^{2}=(a-c)^{2}$.  Because $a\ge b\ge c$, we have $a-c = (a-b)+(b-c)$, whence  

\[
(a-c)^{2} \ge (a-b)^{2}+(b-c)^{2},
\]

and also $a+c-b\ge 0$.  Consequently  

\[
(c-a)^{2}(c+a-b) \ge \bigl[(a-b)^{2}+(b-c)^{2}\bigr](a+c-b).
\]

Insert this estimate into the right‑hand side of (12):

\[
\begin{aligned}
2\bigl(\cdots\bigr)
&\ge (a-b)^{2}(a+b-c)+(b-c)^{2}(b+c-a)
    +\bigl[(a-b)^{2}+(b-c)^{2}\bigr](a+c-b)\\[1mm]
&= (a-b)^{2}\bigl[(a+b-c)+(a+c-b)\bigr]
   +(b-c)^{2}\bigl[(b+c-a)+(a+c-b)\bigr] \\[1mm]
&= (a-b)^{2}\cdot 2a + (b-c)^{2}\cdot 2c \;\ge\; 0.
\end{aligned}
\]

Thus the left‑hand side of (12) is non‑negative, which proves the inequality. $\square$

---
From Schur’s inequality we obtain a convenient bound for $q$.  Using the well‑known identities  

\[
a^{3}+b^{3}+c^{3} = p^{3}-3pq+3r,\qquad
\sum_{\text{sym}}a^{2}b = S+U = pq-3r,
\]

Schur’s inequality becomes  

\[
(p^{3}-3pq+3r)+3r \ge pq-3r
\;\Longrightarrow\; p^{3}+9r \ge 4pq.
\]

With $p=3$ this yields  

\[
27+9r \ge 12q \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
q \le \frac{27+9r}{12}= \frac{9+3r}{4}. \tag{13}
\]

---
Now we return to $P$.  From $S+U = pq-3r = 3q-3r$ we get $U = 3q-3r-S$.  Substituting this into $S+rU$:

\[
\begin{aligned}
S+rU &= S + r(3q-3r-S) \\
     &= S(1-r) + 3rq - 3r^{2}. \tag{14}
\end{aligned}
\]

All quantities are non‑negative; moreover $r = abc \le \bigl(\frac{a+b+c}{3}\bigr)^{3}=1$, hence $1-r\ge 0$.

Using Lemma 1 ($S\le 4$) and the estimate (13) for $q$ in (14) we obtain  

\[
\begin{aligned}
S+rU &\le 4(1-r) + 3r\cdot\frac{9+3r}{4} - 3r^{2} \\
     &= 4 - 4r + \frac{27r+9r^{2}}{4} - 3r^{2} \\
     &= 4 + \frac{11r}{4} - \frac{3r^{2}}{4}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Finally, from (8),

\[
\begin{aligned}
P &= 1 + (S+rU) + r^{3} \\
  &\le 1 + \Bigl(4 + \frac{11r}{4} - \frac{3r^{2}}{4}\Bigr) + r^{3} \\
  &= 5 + \frac{11r}{4} - \frac{3r^{2}}{4} + r^{3}. \tag{15}
\end{aligned}
\]

It remains to verify that the right‑hand side of (15) does not exceed $5+3r$:

\[
5 + \frac{11r}{4} - \frac{3r^{2}}{4} + r^{3} \le 5+3r
\;\Longleftrightarrow\;
\frac{11r}{4} - \frac{3r^{2}}{4} + r^{3} \le 3r.
\]

Multiplying by $4$ and rearranging,

\[
11r - 3r^{2} + 4r^{3} \le 12r
\;\Longleftrightarrow\;
4r^{3} - 3r^{2} - r \le 0
\;\Longleftrightarrow\;
r(4r^{2}-3r-1) \le 0.
\]

Since $r\ge 0$, this is equivalent to $4r^{2}-3r-1\le 0$.  Factorising,

\[
4r^{2}-3r-1 = (4r+1)(r-1).
\]

Because $r\ge 0$, we have $4r+1>0$; therefore $4r^{2}-3r-1\le 0$ holds precisely when $r\le 1$.  And indeed $r = abc \le \bigl(\frac{a+b+c}{3}\bigr)^{3}=1$ by the AM–GM inequality.  Consequently  

\[
4r^{3}-3r^{2}-r \le 0,
\]

and from (15) we obtain $P \le 5+3r = 5+3abc$.  This completes the proof of part (2).

\|\mathbf{w}+\mathbf{u}\|^{2} &= z^{2}+x^{2}-zx,\\[2mm]
\|\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}+\mathbf{w}\|^{2} &= x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}
      +2(\mathbf{u}\!\cdot\!\mathbf{v}+\mathbf{v}\!\cdot\!\mathbf{w}+\mathbf{w}\!\cdot\!\mathbf{u})\\
      &= x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}-(xy+yz+zx).
\end{aligned}
\]

Hence  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\|\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}\| &= \sqrt{x^{2}-xy+y^{2}},\\
\|\mathbf{v}+\mathbf{w}\| &= \sqrt{y^{2}-yz+z^{2}},\\
\|\mathbf{w}+\mathbf{u}\| &= \sqrt{z^{2}-zx+x^{2}},\\
\|\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}+\mathbf{w}\| &= \sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}-xy-yz-zx}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Therefore the required inequality becomes  

\[
\|\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}\|+\|\mathbf{v}+\mathbf{w}\|+\|\mathbf{w}+\mathbf{u}\|
\le \|\mathbf{u}\|+\|\mathbf{v}\|+\|\mathbf{w}\|+\|\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}+\mathbf{w}\|. \tag{1}
\]

Inequality (1) is exactly **Hlawka’s inequality** for three vectors.  
We prove it in full generality.

> **Hlawka’s inequality.** For any vectors \(\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b},\mathbf{c}\) in an inner‑product space,
> \[
> \|\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}\|+\|\mathbf{b}+\mathbf{c}\|+\|\mathbf{c}+\mathbf{a}\|
> \le \|\mathbf{a}\|+\|\mathbf{b}\|+\|\mathbf{c}\|+\|\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}+\mathbf{c}\|.
> \]

*Proof.*  Set  

\[
S = \|\mathbf{a}\|+\|\mathbf{b}\|+\|\mathbf{c}\|,\qquad
P = \|\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}\|+\|\mathbf{b}+\mathbf{c}\|+\|\mathbf{c}+\mathbf{a}\|,\qquad
T = \|\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}+\mathbf{c}\|.
\]

If \(S=T=0\) then all vectors are \(\mathbf{0}\) and the inequality is trivial; therefore we assume \(S+T>0\).

For any two vectors \(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\),

\[
(\|\mathbf{x}\|+\|\mathbf{y}\|)^{2}-\|\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{y}\|^{2}
   = 2\bigl(\|\mathbf{x}\|\|\mathbf{y}\|-\mathbf{x}\!\cdot\!\mathbf{y}\bigr). \tag{2}
\]

The left‑hand side factors as  

\[
(\|\mathbf{x}\|+\|\mathbf{y}\|-\|\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{y}\|)
(\|\mathbf{x}\|+\|\mathbf{y}\|+\|\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{y}\|).
\]

Denote \(A_{\mathbf{x}\mathbf{y}} = \|\mathbf{x}\|+\|\mathbf{y}\|+\|\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{y}\|\); then  

\[
(\|\mathbf{x}\|+\|\mathbf{y}\|-\|\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{y}\|)\,A_{\mathbf{x}\mathbf{y}}
   = 2\bigl(\|\mathbf{x}\|\|\mathbf{y}\|-\mathbf{x}\!\cdot\!\mathbf{y}\bigr). \tag{3}
\]

Apply this to the three pairs \((\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b}),(\mathbf{b},\mathbf{c}),(\mathbf{c},\mathbf{a})\) and write  

\[
A = A_{\mathbf{a}\mathbf{b}},\qquad B = A_{\mathbf{b}\mathbf{c}},\qquad C = A_{\mathbf{c}\mathbf{a}}.
\]

From the triangle inequality,

\[
\|\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}\| = \|(\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}+\mathbf{c})-\mathbf{c}\|
                        \le \|\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}+\mathbf{c}\| + \|\mathbf{c}\|,
\]

hence  

\[
A = \|\mathbf{a}\|+\|\mathbf{b}\|+\|\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}\|
   \le \|\mathbf{a}\|+\|\mathbf{b}\|+\|\mathbf{c}\|+\|\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}+\mathbf{c}\|
   = S+T.
\]

The same estimate gives \(B\le S+T\) and \(C\le S+T\).

Now consider the pair \((\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b})\).  
If \(A=0\), then \(\mathbf{a}=\mathbf{b}=\mathbf{0}\); consequently \(\|\mathbf{a}\|+\|\mathbf{b}\|-\|\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}\|=0\) and \(\|\mathbf{a}\|\|\mathbf{b}\|-\mathbf{a}\!\cdot\!\mathbf{b}=0\), so the inequality  

\[
\|\mathbf{a}\|+\|\mathbf{b}\|-\|\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}\|
   \ge \frac{2\bigl(\|\mathbf{a}\|\|\mathbf{b}\|-\mathbf{a}\!\cdot\!\mathbf{b}\bigr)}{S+T} \tag{4}
\]

holds trivially (both sides are \(0\)).  
If \(A>0\), then from (3)

\[
\|\mathbf{a}\|+\|\mathbf{b}\|-\|\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}\|
   = \frac{2\bigl(\|\mathbf{a}\|\|\mathbf{b}\|-\mathbf{a}\!\cdot\!\mathbf{b}\bigr)}{A}.
\]

Because \(A\le S+T\) and \(\|\mathbf{a}\|\|\mathbf{b}\|-\mathbf{a}\!\cdot\!\mathbf{b}\ge0\), we obtain  

\[
\frac{2\bigl(\|\mathbf{a}\|\|\mathbf{b}\|-\mathbf{a}\!\cdot\!\mathbf{b}\bigr)}{A}
   \ge \frac{2\bigl(\|\mathbf{a}\|\|\mathbf{b}\|-\mathbf{a}\!\cdot\!\mathbf{b}\bigr)}{S+T},
\]

which is exactly (4).  The same reasoning yields analogous inequalities for the pairs \((\mathbf{b},\mathbf{c})\) and \((\mathbf{c},\mathbf{a})\).  Adding the three inequalities of type (4) gives  

\[
\sum_{\text{cyc}}\bigl(\|\mathbf{a}\|+\|\mathbf{b}\|-\|\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}\|\bigr)
   \ge \frac{2\sum_{\text{cyc}}\bigl(\|\mathbf{a}\|\|\mathbf{b}\|-\mathbf{a}\!\cdot\!\mathbf{b}\bigr)}{S+T}. \tag{5}
\]

(The cyclic sum runs over \((\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b}),(\mathbf{b},\mathbf{c}),(\mathbf{c},\mathbf{a})\).)

Next compute \(S^{2}-T^{2}\):

\[
\begin{aligned}
S^{2}-T^{2}
&= (\|\mathbf{a}\|+\|\mathbf{b}\|+\|\mathbf{c}\|)^{2}
   - \|\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}+\mathbf{c}\|^{2} \\
&= 2\Bigl(\|\mathbf{a}\|\|\mathbf{b}\|-\mathbf{a}\!\cdot\!\mathbf{b}
          +\|\mathbf{b}\|\|\mathbf{c}\|-\mathbf{b}\!\cdot\!\mathbf{c}
          +\|\mathbf{c}\|\|\mathbf{a}\|-\mathbf{c}\!\cdot\!\mathbf{a}\Bigr). \tag{6}
\end{aligned}
\]

Since \(S+T>0\),

\[
S-T = \frac{S^{2}-T^{2}}{S+T}
     = \frac{2\sum_{\text{cyc}}\bigl(\|\mathbf{a}\|\|\mathbf{b}\|-\mathbf{a}\!\cdot\!\mathbf{b}\bigr)}{S+T}. \tag{7}
\]

Combining (5) and (7) we obtain  

\[
\sum_{\text{cyc}}\bigl(\|\mathbf{a}\|+\|\mathbf{b}\|-\|\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}\|\bigr) \ge S-T.
\]

The left‑hand side equals  

\[
\bigl(\|\mathbf{a}\|+\|\mathbf{b}\|\bigr)+\bigl(\|\mathbf{b}\|+\|\mathbf{c}\|\bigr)+\bigl(\|\mathbf{c}\|+\|\mathbf{a}\|\bigr) - P
   = 2S-P.
\]

Hence \(2S-P \ge S-T\), i.e. \(P \le S+T\), which is exactly Hlawka’s inequality. \(\square\)

Applying the proved inequality to the vectors \(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v},\mathbf{w}\) gives (1), and therefore  

\[
\sqrt{x^{2}-xy+y^{2}}+\sqrt{y^{2}-yz+z^{2}}+\sqrt{z^{2}-zx+x^{2}}
\le x+y+z+\sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}-xy-yz-zx},
\]

which completes the proof of part (1).

### 2. Second inequality  

Let \(a,b,c\ge 0\) with \(a+b+c=3\).  Set  

\[
p = a+b+c = 3,\qquad
q = ab+bc+ca,\qquad
r = abc.
\]

Introduce the two cyclic sums  

\[
S = a^{2}b + b^{2}c + c^{2}a,\qquad
U = a b^{2} + b c^{2} + c a^{2}.
\]

First expand the product:

\[
\begin{aligned}
P &:= (1+a^{2}b)(1+b^{2}c)(1+c^{2}a) \\
  &= 1 + (a^{2}b+b^{2}c+c^{2}a) \\

     + (a^{2}b)(b^{2}c)(c^{2}a)\\[2mm]
  &= 1 + S + \bigl(a^{2}b^{3}c + b^{2}c^{3}a + c^{2}a^{3}b\bigr) + (abc)^{3}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Notice that  

\[
a^{2}b^{3}c = abc\cdot a b^{2},\quad
b^{2}c^{3}a = abc\cdot b c^{2},\quad
c^{2}a^{3}b = abc\cdot c a^{2}.
\]

Hence  

\[
a^{2}b^{3}c + b^{2}c^{3}a + c^{2}a^{3}b = r\,U,
\]

and therefore  

\[
P = 1 + S + rU + r^{3}. \tag{8}
\]

**Lemma 1.** \(S \le 4\).

*Proof.*  Consider the function \(f(a,b,c)=a^{2}b+b^{2}c+c^{2}a\) on the compact set  

\[
D = \{\, (a,b,c)\in\mathbb{R}^{3}\mid a,b,c\ge 0,\ a+b+c=3 \,\}.
\]

\(f\) is continuous, so it attains a maximum on \(D\).

If the maximum occurs at an interior point (all coordinates \(>0\)), then by Lagrange multipliers there exists \(\lambda\) such that  

\[
\frac{\partial f}{\partial a}=2ab+c^{2}= \lambda,\qquad
\frac{\partial f}{\partial b}=a^{2}+2bc= \lambda,\qquad
\frac{\partial f}{\partial c}=b^{2}+2ca= \lambda. \tag{9}
\]

From the first two equalities,

\[
2ab+c^{2}=a^{2}+2bc \;\Longrightarrow\; 2ab-a^{2}=2bc-c^{2}
\;\Longrightarrow\; a(2b-a)=c(2b-c). \tag{10}
\]

From the second and third equalities,

\[
a^{2}+2bc = b^{2}+2ca \;\Longrightarrow\; a^{2}-b^{2}=2c(a-b)
\;\Longrightarrow\; (a-b)(a+b-2c)=0. \tag{11}
\]

If \(a\neq b\), then \(a+b=2c\).  Substitute \(c=\dfrac{a+b}{2}\) into (10):

\[
a(2b-a) = \frac{a+b}{2}\Bigl(2b-\frac{a+b}{2}\Bigr)
        = \frac{(a+b)(3b-a)}{4}.
\]

Multiplying by \(4\) and expanding gives  

\[
4a(2b-a) = (a+b)(3b-a)
\;\Longrightarrow\; 8ab-4a^{2}=2ab-a^{2}+3b^{2}
\;\Longrightarrow\; 6ab-3a^{2}-3b^{2}=0,
\]

i.e. \(2ab-a^{2}-b^{2}=0\), which is \(-(a-b)^{2}=0\); hence \(a=b\), contradicting \(a\neq b\).  Thus \(a=b\).

Now with \(a=b\), the first and third equations in (9) become  

\[
2a^{2}+c^{2}= \lambda,\qquad a^{2}+2ca = \lambda.
\]

Equating them yields \(2a^{2}+c^{2}=a^{2}+2ca\), i.e. \(a^{2}-2ca+c^{2}=0\), so \((a-c)^{2}=0\) and \(a=c\).  Consequently \(a=b=c\).

Thus the only possible interior critical point is \(a=b=c=1\), where \(f=3\).

If the maximum lies on the boundary of \(D\), then at least one variable equals \(0\).  The function \(f\) is invariant under cyclic permutations of \((a,b,c)\); therefore we may assume \(c=0\) (otherwise rotate the triple).  Then \(a+b=3\) and  

\[
f = a^{2}b.
\]

By the AM–GM inequality,

\[
a^{2}b = 4\cdot\frac{a}{2}\cdot\frac{a}{2}\cdot b
       \le 4\Bigl(\frac{\frac{a}{2}+\frac{a}{2}+b}{3}\Bigr)^{\!3}
       = 4\Bigl(\frac{a+b}{3}\Bigr)^{\!3}
       = 4\cdot 1^{3}=4.
\]

Equality holds when \(\dfrac{a}{2}=b\), i.e. \(a=2,\ b=1\).  Hence on the boundary \(f\le 4\).

Comparing the interior candidate (\(3\)) with the boundary maximum (\(4\)) we conclude that the global maximum of \(f\) on \(D\) is \(4\).  Therefore \(S=f(a,b,c)\le 4\) for all \((a,b,c)\in D\).  \(\square\)

**Lemma 2 (Schur’s inequality).** For \(a,b,c\ge 0\),

\[
a^{3}+b^{3}+c^{3}+3abc \ge \sum_{\text{sym}}a^{2}b,
\]

where \(\displaystyle\sum_{\text{sym}}a^{2}b = a^{2}b+a^{2}c+b^{2}a+b^{2}c+c^{2}a+c^{2}b\).

*Proof.*  The inequality is symmetric, so we may assume \(a\ge b\ge c\ge 0\).  One can verify the identity  

\[
2\bigl(a^{3}+b^{3}+c^{3}+3abc-\sum_{\text{sym}}a^{2}b\bigr)
= (a-b)^{2}(a+b-c)+(b-c)^{2}(b+c-a)+(c-a)^{2}(c+a-b). \tag{12}
\]

Now \((c-a)^{2}=(a-c)^{2}\).  Because \(a\ge b\ge c\), we have \(a-c = (a-b)+(b-c)\), whence  

\[
(a-c)^{2} \ge (a-b)^{2}+(b-c)^{2},
\]

and also \(a+c-b\ge 0\).  Consequently  

\[
(c-a)^{2}(c+a-b) \ge \bigl[(a-b)^{2}+(b-c)^{2}\bigr](a+c-b).
\]

Insert this estimate into the right‑hand side of (12):

\[
\begin{aligned}
2\bigl(\cdots\bigr)
&\ge (a-b)^{2}(a+b-c)+(b-c)^{2}(b+c-a)
    +\bigl[(a-b)^{2}+(b-c)^{2}\bigr](a+c-b)\\[1mm]
&= (a-b)^{2}\bigl[(a+b-c)+(a+c-b)\bigr]
   +(b-c)^{2}\bigl[(b+c-a)+(a+c-b)\bigr] \\[1mm]
&= (a-b)^{2}\cdot 2a + (b-c)^{2}\cdot 2c \;\ge\; 0.
\end{aligned}
\]

Thus the left‑hand side of (12) is non‑negative, which proves the inequality. \(\square\)

---
From Schur’s inequality we obtain a convenient bound for \(q\).  Using the well‑known identities  

\[
a^{3}+b^{3}+c^{3} = p^{3}-3pq+3r,\qquad
\sum_{\text{sym}}a^{2}b = S+U = pq-3r,
\]

Schur’s inequality becomes  

\[
(p^{3}-3pq+3r)+3r \ge pq-3r
\;\Longrightarrow\; p^{3}+9r \ge 4pq.
\]

With \(p=3\) this yields  

\[
27+9r \ge 12q \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
q \le \frac{27+9r}{12}= \frac{9+3r}{4}. \tag{13}
\]

---
Now we return to \(P\).  From \(S+U = pq-3r = 3q-3r\) we get \(U = 3q-3r-S\).  Substituting this into \(S+rU\):

\[
\begin{aligned}
S+rU &= S + r(3q-3r-S) \\
     &= S(1-r) + 3rq - 3r^{2}. \tag{14}
\end{aligned}
\]

All quantities are non‑negative; moreover \(r = abc \le \bigl(\frac{a+b+c}{3}\bigr)^{3}=1\), hence \(1-r\ge 0\).

Using Lemma 1 (\(S\le 4\)) and the estimate (13) for \(q\) in (14) we obtain  

\[
\begin{aligned}
S+rU &\le 4(1-r) + 3r\cdot\frac{9+3r}{4} - 3r^{2} \\
     &= 4 - 4r + \frac{27r+9r^{2}}{4} - 3r^{2} \\
     &= 4 + \frac{11r}{4} - \frac{3r^{2}}{4}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Finally, from (8),

\[
\begin{aligned}
P &= 1 + (S+rU) + r^{3} \\
  &\le 1 + \Bigl(4 + \frac{11r}{4} - \frac{3r^{2}}{4}\Bigr) + r^{3} \\
  &= 5 + \frac{11r}{4} - \frac{3r^{2}}{4} + r^{3}. \tag{15}
\end{aligned}
\]

It remains to verify that the right‑hand side of (15) does not exceed \(5+3r\):

\[
5 + \frac{11r}{4} - \frac{3r^{2}}{4} + r^{3} \le 5+3r
\;\Longleftrightarrow\;
\frac{11r}{4} - \frac{3r^{2}}{4} + r^{3} \le 3r.
\]

Multiplying by \(4\) and rearranging,

\[
11r - 3r^{2} + 4r^{3} \le 12r
\;\Longleftrightarrow\;
4r^{3} - 3r^{2} - r \le 0
\;\Longleftrightarrow\;
r(4r^{2}-3r-1) \le 0.
\]

Since \(r\ge 0\), this is equivalent to \(4r^{2}-3r-1\le 0\).  Factorising,

\[
4r^{2}-3r-1 = (4r+1)(r-1).
\]

Because \(r\ge 0\), we have \(4r+1>0\); therefore \(4r^{2}-3r-1\le 0\) holds precisely when \(r\le 1\).  And indeed \(r = abc \le \bigl(\frac{a+b+c}{3}\bigr)^{3}=1\) by the AM–GM inequality.  Consequently  

\[
4r^{3}-3r^{2}-r \le 0,
\]

and from (15) we obtain \(P \le 5+3r = 5+3abc\).  This completes the proof of part (2).

\[

*Step 2 – another Cauchy–Schwarz.*  

\[
D=\sum_{\text{cyc}}\sqrt{x}\;\sqrt{x(x^{2}+8k yz)}
   \le\sqrt{\sum x}\;\sqrt{\sum x(x^{2}+8k yz)}
   =\sqrt{S}\,\sqrt{T}.
\]

Hence \(D^{2}\le S\,T\), i.e. \(\displaystyle\frac{T}{D^{2}}\ge\frac1S\).

*Step 3 – combining the estimates.*  

\[
A^{2}T\;\ge\;\frac{S^{4}}{D^{2}}\,T
        \;\ge\;S^{4}\cdot\frac1S = S^{3},

A\;\ge\;\frac{S^{3/2}}{\sqrt{T}}. \tag{3}
\]

*Step 4 – reducing to an algebraic inequality.*  
Because of (3), to obtain (2) it is enough to show  

\[
\frac{S^{3/2}}{\sqrt{T}}\ge\frac{3}{\sqrt{1+8k}}

S^{3}(1+8k)\ge 9T. \tag{4}
\]

\[
S^{3}=(x+y+z)^{3}= \sum x^{3}+3\sum_{\text{cyc}} xy(x+y)+6xyz .

Therefore  

\[
S^{3}(1+8k)= (1+8k)\sum x^{3}+3(1+8k)\sum xy(x+y)+6(1+8k)xyz .
\]

A simple AM–GM argument gives  

\[
\sum_{\text{cyc}} xy(x+y)\ge 6xyz .
\tag{5}
\]

(Indeed, \(x^{2}y+xy^{2}\ge2x^{3/2}y^{3/2}\); summing cyclically and applying AM–GM to \((xy)^{3/2},(yz)^{3/2},(zx)^{3/2}\) yields the bound.)

### 2.  Team inequality (inequality in a triangle)  

Let \(a,b,c\) be the side lengths, \(p=\dfrac{a+b+c}{2}\) the semiperimeter, \(S\) the area, and \(r=\dfrac{S}{p}\) the inradius.  The altitudes are  

\[
h_{a}=\frac{2S}{a},\quad h_{b}=\frac{2S}{b},\quad h_{c}=\frac{2S}{c}.
\]

Denote  

\[
T = a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}-ab-bc-ca\;\;(\ge 0).
\]

The inequality to prove is  

\[
h_{a}+h_{b}+h_{c}\;\le\;9r+\frac{T}{p}.
\]

Substituting the expressions above,

\[
2S\Bigl(\frac1a+\frac1b+\frac1c\Bigr)
   \le 9\cdot\frac{S}{p}+\frac{T}{p}.
\]

Multiply by \(p\) and use \(2p=a+b+c\):

\[
S(a+b+c)\Bigl(\frac1a+\frac1b+\frac1c\Bigr) \le 9S + T. \tag{6}
\]

Because \(\displaystyle\frac1a+\frac1b+\frac1c=\frac{ab+bc+ca}{abc}\), (6) becomes  

\[
S\,\frac{(a+b+c)(ab+bc+ca)}{abc}\le 9S+T.
\]

Dividing by the positive area \(S\),

\[
\frac{(a+b+c)(ab+bc+ca)}{abc}\le 9+\frac{T}{S}. \tag{7}
\]

Now expand the numerator:

\[
(a+b+c)(ab+bc+ca)=\sum_{\text{sym}}a^{2}b+3abc .
\]

Hence the left‑hand side of (7) equals  

\[
\frac{\sum_{\text{sym}}a^{2}b}{abc}+3
   =\sum_{\text{sym}}\frac{a}{b}+3 .
\]

The symmetric sum of ratios can be rewritten with squares:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{\text{sym}}\frac{a}{b}
&=\sum_{\text{cyc}}\Bigl(\frac{a}{b}+\frac{b}{a}\Bigr)   \\
&=\sum_{\text{cyc}}\Bigl(2+\frac{(a-b)^{2}}{ab}\Bigr)   \\
&=6+\sum_{\text{cyc}}\frac{(a-b)^{2}}{ab}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Therefore the left‑hand side of (7) is \(9+\displaystyle\sum_{\text{cyc}}\frac{(a-b)^{2}}{ab}\), and (7) simplifies to  

\[
\sum_{\text{cyc}}\frac{(a-b)^{2}}{ab}\;\le\;\frac{T}{S}. \tag{8}
\]

Recall that  

\[
T=\frac12\bigl((a-b)^{2}+(b-c)^{2}+(c-a)^{2}\bigr).
\]

Thus (8) is equivalent to  

\[
2S\sum_{\text{cyc}}\frac{(a-b)^{2}}{ab}\;\le\;\sum_{\text{cyc}}(a-b)^{2}. \tag{9}
\]

To prove (9) we use the elementary area bound: for any triangle,
\(S=\frac12 ab\sin C\le\frac12 ab\); hence \(2S\le ab\).  Similarly \(2S\le bc\) and \(2S\le ca\).  Consequently  

\[
\begin{aligned}
(a-b)^{2}&\ge (a-b)^{2}\cdot\frac{2S}{ab},\\
(b-c)^{2}&\ge (b-c)^{2}\cdot\frac{2S}{bc},\\
(c-a)^{2}&\ge (c-a)^{2}\cdot\frac{2S}{ca}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Adding these three inequalities yields exactly (9).  

Since (9) holds, we obtain (8) and finally the original inequality.  Equality occurs iff \(a=b=c\) (equilateral triangle), which indeed gives \(h_{a}+h_{b}+h_{c}=9r\) and \(T=0\).  \(\square\)

#### (b)
**1. A useful estimate.** For any non‑negative $b,c$ we have $(b+c)\sqrt{bc}\ge 2bc$ because $b+c\ge 2\sqrt{bc}$ by AM–GM. Hence
\[
\sqrt{bc}\ge\frac{2bc}{b+c},
\]
with equality iff $b=c$. Consequently
\[
a+\sqrt{bc}\ge a+\frac{2bc}{b+c}= \frac{ab+ac+2bc}{b+c},
\]
and therefore
\[
\frac{4}{a+\sqrt{bc}}\le\frac{4(b+c)}{ab+2bc+ca}. \tag{1}
\]

Summing the three cyclic analogues we obtain
\[
\sum_{\text{cyc}}\frac{4}{a+\sqrt{bc}}
\le 4\sum_{\text{cyc}}\frac{b+c}{ab+2bc+ca}. \tag{2}
\]

Denote the right–hand side of (2) by $L$.  If we prove $L\le a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}+ab+bc+ca$, the desired inequality follows.

**2. A convenient substitution.**  Because the inequality is symmetric and the case when one of the numbers equals $0$ reduces directly to part (a) (see the remark at the end), we may assume $a,b,c>0$.  Set
\[
x=\frac1a,\qquad y=\frac1b,\qquad z=\frac1c .
\]
Then $x,y,z>0$.  A short computation gives
\[
\frac{b+c}{ab+2bc+ca}= \frac{x(y+z)}{2x+y+z},
\]
and cyclically.  Hence
\[
L = 4\sum_{\text{cyc}}\frac{x(y+z)}{2x+y+z}. \tag{3}
\]

The condition $(a+b)(b+c)(c+a)=8$ becomes
\[
\frac{(x+y)(y+z)(z+x)}{x^{2}y^{2}z^{2}}=8
\;\Longleftrightarrow\;
(x+y)(y+z)(z+x)=8(xyz)^{2}. \tag{4}
\]

The right–hand side of the required inequality turns into
\[
a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}+ab+bc+ca
= \frac1{x^{2}}+\frac1{y^{2}}+\frac1{z^{2}}
   +\frac1{xy}+\frac1{yz}+\frac1{zx}. \tag{5}
\]

Introduce the symmetric sums
\[
S=x+y+z,\qquad Q=xy+yz+zx,\qquad P=xyz\;(>0).
\]
Then $(x+y)(y+z)(z+x)=SQ-P$, and (4) rewrites as
\[
SQ-P = 8P^{2}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad SQ = P(1+8P). \tag{6}
\]

Moreover
\[
\frac1{x^{2}}+\frac1{y^{2}}+\frac1{z^{2}} = \frac{Q^{2}-2PS}{P^{2}},\qquad
\frac1{xy}+\frac1{yz}+\frac1{zx}= \frac{S}{P},
\]
so that
\[
a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}+ab+bc+ca = \frac{Q^{2}}{P^{2}}-\frac{S}{P}. \tag{7}
\]

**3. Expressing $L$ through $S,Q,P$.**  Observe that
\[
\frac{x(y+z)}{2x+y+z}= \frac{x(S-x)}{S+x}.
\]
Indeed $y+z=S-x$ and $2x+y+z=S+x$.  Summing cyclically,
\[
\sum_{\text{cyc}}\frac{x(S-x)}{S+x}
= \sum_{\text{cyc}}\Bigl(x-\frac{2x^{2}}{S+x}\Bigr)
= S-2\sum_{\text{cyc}}\frac{x^{2}}{S+x}. \tag{8}
\]

To handle the last sum put
\[
U=\sum_{\text{cyc}}\frac{x}{S+x}.
\]
Since $\displaystyle\frac{x^{2}}{S+x}=x-\frac{xS}{S+x}$, we obtain
\[
\sum_{\text{cyc}}\frac{x^{2}}{S+x}=S-SU. \tag{9}
\]
Substituting (9) into (8) yields
\[
\sum_{\text{cyc}}\frac{x(S-x)}{S+x}=S-2(S-SU)=2SU-S. \tag{10}
\]

Now we compute $U$.  Writing the three fractions with the common denominator
$(S+x)(S+y)(S+z)$,
\[
U=\frac{\sum x(S+y)(S+z)}{(S+x)(S+y)(S+z)}.
\]
Because $(S+x)(S+y)(S+z)=2S^{3}+SQ+P$ and
\[
\sum x(S+y)(S+z)=S^{3}+2SQ+3P
\]
(a straightforward expansion), we get
\[
U=\frac{S^{3}+2SQ+3P}{2S^{3}+SQ+P}. \tag{11}
\]

From (3) and (10) we have $L=4(2SU-S)=4S(2U-1)$.  Using (11),
\[
2U-1=\frac{2(S^{3}+2SQ+3P)-(2S^{3}+SQ+P)}{2S^{3}+SQ+P}
      =\frac{3SQ+5P}{2S^{3}+SQ+P},
\]
hence
\[
L = 4S\cdot\frac{3SQ+5P}{2S^{3}+SQ+P}. \tag{12}
\]

**4. Using the condition.**  From (6) we have $SQ = P(1+8P)$.  Insert this into (12):
\[
3SQ+5P = 3P(1+8P)+5P = P(3+24P+5)=8P(3P+1),
\]
\[
2S^{3}+SQ+P = 2S^{3}+P(1+8P)+P = 2S^{3}+P(8P+2)=2\bigl(S^{3}+P(4P+1)\bigr).
\]
Therefore
\[
L = 4S\cdot\frac{8P(3P+1)}{2\bigl(S^{3}+P(4P+1)\bigr)}
    = \frac{16\,S\,P\,(3P+1)}{S^{3}+P(4P+1)}. \tag{13}
\]

The right–hand side (7) together with $Q^{2}= \dfrac{P^{2}(1+8P)^{2}}{S^{2}}$ (from $SQ=P(1+8P)$) becomes
\[
R:= \frac{Q^{2}}{P^{2}}-\frac{S}{P}
    = \frac{(1+8P)^{2}}{S^{2}}-\frac{S}{P}. \tag{14}
\]

Thus we have to prove
\[
\frac{16\,S\,P\,(3P+1)}{S^{3}+P(4P+1)} \le \frac{(1+8P)^{2}}{S^{2}}-\frac{S}{P}. \tag{15}
\]

**5. Eliminating $S$ in favour of $A=S^{3}$.**  Set
\[
A = S^{3},\qquad B = P\;(>0).
\]
Notice that $S^{2}=A^{2/3}$; to avoid fractional exponents we multiply (15) by the positive quantity $\bigl(A+B(4B+1)\bigr)\,B\,S^{2}$.  The left‑hand side becomes
\[
\frac{16\,S\,B\,(3B+1)}{A+B(4B+1)}\cdot B\,S^{2}
= 16\,A\,B^{2}(3B+1),
\]
while the right‑hand side gives
\[
\Bigl(\frac{(1+8B)^{2}}{S^{2}}-\frac{S}{B}\Bigr)\bigl(A+B(4B+1)\bigr)B\,S^{2}
= \bigl(B(1+8B)^{2}-A\bigr)\bigl(A+B(4B+1)\bigr).
\]

Consequently (15) is equivalent to
\[
16\,A\,B^{2}(3B+1) \le \bigl(B(1+8B)^{2}-A\bigr)\bigl(A+B(4B+1)\bigr). \tag{16}
\]

Define
\[
F(A,B)=\bigl(B(1+8B)^{2}-A\bigr)\bigl(A+B(4B+1)\bigr)-16\,A\,B^{2}(3B+1).
\]
Expanding and collecting the terms containing $A$:
\[
\begin{aligned}
F(A,B) &= -A^{2}
        +A\Bigl[\,B(1+8B)^{2}-B(4B+1)-16B^{2}(3B+1)\Bigr] \\
       &\qquad +B^{2}(1+8B)^{2}(4B+1).
\end{aligned}
\]
The coefficient of $A$ simplifies:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&B(1+8B)^{2}-B(4B+1)-16B^{2}(3B+1)\\
&= B(1+16B+64B^{2})-4B^{2}-B-48B^{3}-16B^{2}\\
&= 16B^{3}-4B^{2}=4B^{2}(4B-1).
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus
\[
F(A,B) = -A^{2}+4A\,B^{2}(4B-1)+B^{2}(1+8B)^{2}(4B+1). \tag{17}
\]

Inequality (16) is exactly $F(A,B)\ge 0$.

**6. When is $F(A,B)\ge 0$?**  Fix $B>0$ and view $F$ as a quadratic in $A$:
\[
F(A)=-A^{2}+4B^{2}(4B-1)A + K,\qquad
K=B^{2}(1+8B)^{2}(4B+1).
\]
The equation $F(A)=0$ is equivalent to $A^{2}-4B^{2}(4B-1)A-K=0$.  Its discriminant is
\[
\Delta_{F}=16B^{4}(4B-1)^{2}+4K
          =4B^{2}\Bigl[\,4B^{2}(4B-1)^{2}+(1+8B)^{2}(4B+1)\Bigr]>0.
\]
The product of the roots equals $-K<0$, therefore the two roots have opposite signs.  The positive root is
\[
r(B)=2B^{2}(4B-1)+B\sqrt{\,4B^{2}(4B-1)^{2}+(1+8B)^{2}(4B+1)\,}. \tag{18}
\]
Since the coefficient of $A^{2}$ in $F$ is negative, $F(A)\ge 0$ precisely for $A$ between the two roots.  Because one root is negative, for $A\ge 0$ this condition is equivalent to
\[
A\le r(B). \tag{19}
\]

Hence proving $F(A,B)\ge 0$ is the same as showing $A\le r(B)$.

**7. An upper bound for $A$ coming from the discriminant of the cubic.**  
The numbers $x,y,z$ are the (positive) roots of
\[
t^{3}-S t^{2}+Q t-P=0. \tag{20}
\]
For a cubic with three real roots its discriminant $\Delta$ is non‑negative.  For $t^{3}+a t^{2}+b t+c$ the discriminant is
\[
\Delta = a^{2}b^{2}-4b^{3}-4a^{3}c-27c^{2}+18abc.
\]
Applying this to (20) with $a=-S,\;b=Q,\;c=-P$ gives
\[
\Delta = S^{2}Q^{2}+18SQP-4S^{3}P-4Q^{3}-27P^{2}\ge 0. \tag{21}
\]

Now use the relation $SQ = P(1+8P)$ obtained in (6).  Set
\[
R = P(1+8P)\;(=SQ).
\]
Then $Q = R/S$, and
\[
S^{2}Q^{2}=R^{2},\qquad 18SQP = 18RP,\qquad
-4Q^{3}= -\frac{4R^{3}}{S^{3}}.
\]
Substituting these into (21) we obtain
\[
\Delta = R^{2}+18RP-4S^{3}P-\frac{4R^{3}}{S^{3}}-27P^{2}\ge 0.
\]
Multiplying by $S^{3}>0$ yields
\[
S^{3}\bigl(R^{2}+18RP-27P^{2}\bigr)-4S^{6}P-4R^{3}\ge 0. \tag{22}
\]

Again put $A=S^{3}$, $B=P$.  Then $S^{6}=A^{2}$ and (22) becomes
\[
-4B A^{2} + \bigl(R^{2}+18RB-27B^{2}\bigr)A -4R^{3}\ge 0. \tag{23}
\]

Recall $R = B(1+8B)$.  Compute the coefficient of $A$:
\[
\begin{aligned}
R^{2}+18RB-27B^{2}
&= B^{2}(1+8B)^{2}+18B^{2}(1+8B)-27B^{2}\\
&= B^{2}\bigl(1+16B+64B^{2}+18+144B-27\bigr)\\
&= B^{2}\bigl(64B^{2}+160B-8\bigr)
   = 8B^{2}\bigl(8B^{2}+20B-1\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]
Denote
\[
D = 8B^{2}+20B-1,\qquad\text{so that}\qquad
R^{2}+18RB-27B^{2}=8B^{2}D. \tag{24}
\]

Inequality (23) is a quadratic inequality in $A$ with negative leading coefficient.  Therefore it holds exactly for $A$ between the two roots of the corresponding equation.  Solving
\[
-4B A^{2}+8B^{2}D A-4R^{3}=0
\;\Longleftrightarrow\;
4B A^{2}-8B^{2}D A+4R^{3}=0,
\]
the (larger) root is
\[
A_{\max}= \frac{8B^{2}D+\sqrt{64B^{4}D^{2}-64B R^{3}}}{8B}
        = B D + \frac{\sqrt{64B^{4}D^{2}-64B R^{3}}}{8B}. \tag{25}
\]

Now $R^{3}=B^{3}(1+8B)^{3}$, hence
\[
64B^{4}D^{2}-64B R^{3}=64B^{4}\bigl(D^{2}-(1+8B)^{3}\bigr).
\]
A direct expansion shows
\[
\begin{aligned}
D^{2}-(1+8B)^{3}
&= (8B^{2}+20B-1)^{2}-(1+8B)^{3}\\
&= 64B^{4}-192B^{3}+192B^{2}-64B\\
&= 64B(B-1)^{3}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus
\[
\sqrt{64B^{4}D^{2}-64B R^{3}}
   = \sqrt{64B^{4}\cdot 64B(B-1)^{3}}
   = 64\,B^{5/2}(B-1)^{3/2},
\]
and consequently
\[
A_{\max}= B D + 8\,B^{3/2}(B-1)^{3/2}
        = B\bigl(8B^{2}+20B-1\bigr) + 8\,B^{3/2}(B-1)^{3/2}. \tag{26}
\]

Because the admissible $A$ must satisfy (23), we obtain the necessary upper bound
\[
A \le A_{\max}. \tag{27}
\]

**8. Comparison of the two bounds.**  
Recall from (19) that we need $A\le r(B)$.  It therefore suffices to prove
\[
A_{\max}\le r(B)\qquad (B\ge 1). \tag{28}
\]
(The inequality $B\ge 1$ follows from $abc\le 1$, which is a consequence of $(a+b)(b+c)(c+a)\ge 8abc$ together with the condition $(a+b)(b+c)(c+a)=8$; indeed $abc\le 1$ and $P=1/(abc)\ge 1$.)

Dividing (28) by $B>0$ we have to show
\[

\;\le\; 2B(4B-1) + \sqrt{4B^{2}(4B-1)^{2}+(1+8B)^{2}(4B+1)}. \tag{29}
\]

Notice that $2B(4B-1)=8B^{2}-2B$.  Cancelling $8B^{2}$ and rearranging,
\[

\;\le\; \sqrt{4B^{2}(4B-1)^{2}+(1+8B)^{2}(4B+1)}. \tag{30}
\]

Both sides are non‑negative for $B\ge 1$; squaring preserves the inequality.  Set
\[

\[
(22B-1)^{2}+16(22B-1)X+64X^{2}\le Y^{2}.

\[

\[
\begin{aligned}

\[
32B\,(13B^{2}-17B+4)\;\ge\;16(22B-1)X,

or, after division by $16$,
\[
2B\,(13B^{2}-17B+4)\;\ge\;(22B-1)X. \tag{32}
\]

For $B\ge 1$ we have $13B^{2}-17B+4=(B-1)(13B-4)\ge 0$, so the left‑hand side of (32) is non‑negative; the right‑hand side is also non‑negative.  Squaring (32) is therefore legitimate and yields the equivalent inequality
\[
4B^{2}(13B^{2}-17B+4)^{2}\;\ge\;(22B-1)^{2}\,B(B-1)^{3}.
\]
Dividing by $B>0$,
\[
4B\,(13B^{2}-17B+4)^{2}\;\ge\;(22B-1)^{2}(B-1)^{3}. \tag{33}
\]

Now we compare both sides by expanding:
\[
\begin{aligned}
(13B^{2}-17B+4)^{2} &= 169B^{4}-442B^{3}+393B^{2}-136B+16,\\
4B\,(13B^{2}-17B+4)^{2} &= 676B^{5}-1768B^{4}+1572B^{3}-544B^{2}+64B,\\[1mm]
(22B-1)^{2} &= 484B^{2}-44B+1,\\
(B-1)^{3} &= B^{3}-3B^{2}+3B-1,\\
(22B-1)^{2}(B-1)^{3} &= 484B^{5}-1496B^{4}+1585B^{3}-619B^{2}+47B-1.
\end{aligned}
\]

Subtracting the latter from the former,
\[
\begin{aligned}
&4B\,(13B^{2}-17B+4)^{2}-(22B-1)^{2}(B-1)^{3}\\
&= 192B^{5}-272B^{4}-13B^{3}+75B^{2}+17B+1.
\end{aligned}
\]

This polynomial factorises nicely:
\[
192B^{5}-272B^{4}-13B^{3}+75B^{2}+17B+1
= (B-1)^{2}\bigl(192B^{3}+112B^{2}+19B+1\bigr). \tag{34}
\]

Indeed, expanding $(B-1)^{2}(192B^{3}+112B^{2}+19B+1)$ reproduces the left‑hand side.  For $B\ge 1$ we have $(B-1)^{2}\ge 0$ and $192B^{3}+112B^{2}+19B+1>0$, hence the whole expression is non‑negative.  Therefore (33) holds true.

Tracing back the chain of equivalent transformations (each step was reversible because we only squared non‑negative quantities and divided by positive numbers), we conclude that (30) is valid, and consequently (28) holds.  Thus
\[
A_{\max}\le r(B). \tag{35}
\]

**9. Completion of the proof.**  
From the discriminant argument we have $A\le A_{\max}$ (inequality (27)).  Together with (35) this gives $A\le r(B)$.  By the discussion in Step 6, $A\le r(B)$ is equivalent to $F(A,B)\ge 0$, i.e. inequality (16).  Because (16) is exactly the cross‑multiplied form of (15), we obtain $L\le R$ where $R$ is the right‑hand side of (14). \[
\sum_{\text{cyc}}\frac{4}{a+\sqrt{bc}}
\;\le\; a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}+ab+bc+ca
\]
for all $a,b,c>0$ satisfying $(a+b)(b+c)(c+a)=8$.

**10. The case when some variable is zero.**  
If one of $a,b,c$ equals $0$, say $a=0$, then the condition $(a+b)(b+c)(c+a)=8$ becomes $b\,(b+c)\,c =8$, i.e. $bc(b+c)=8$.  In this situation the left‑hand side of the desired inequality reduces to
\[
\frac{4}{\sqrt{bc}}+\frac{4}{b}+\frac{4}{c},
\]
while the right‑hand side becomes $b^{2}+c^{2}+bc$.  But this is exactly the inequality proved in part (a) for the pair $(b,c)$, hence it holds.  The cases $b=0$ or $c=0$ are analogous.  If two variables were zero, the product $(a+b)(b+c)(c+a)$ would be $0$, contradicting the condition.  Thus the inequality is also true when some variables vanish.

Consequently the inequality is valid for all $a,b,c\ge 0$ with $(a+b)(b+c)(c+a)=8$.  This completes the proof of part (b).

## Solution  

### (a)  
Let  

\[
u=\sqrt{ab}>0,\qquad v=a+b>0 .
\]

Then \(ab=u^{2}\) and \(a+b=v\).  The condition \(ab(a+b)=8\) becomes  

\[
u^{2}v=8\quad\Longrightarrow\quad v=\frac{8}{u^{2}} .
\]

Now  

\[
\frac{4}{\sqrt{ab}}+\frac{4}{a}+\frac{4}{b}
   =\frac{4}{u}+\frac{4(a+b)}{ab}
   =\frac{4}{u}+\frac{4v}{u^{2}},
\]

\[
a^{2}+b^{2}+ab=(a+b)^{2}-ab=v^{2}-u^{2}.
\]

Substituting \(v=8/u^{2}\),

\[
\frac{4}{\sqrt{ab}}+\frac{4}{a}+\frac{4}{b}
   =\frac{4}{u}+\frac{32}{u^{4}},\qquad
a^{2}+b^{2}+ab=\frac{64}{u^{4}}-u^{2}.
\]

The required inequality is therefore  

\[
\frac{4}{u}+\frac{32}{u^{4}}\le\frac{64}{u^{4}}-u^{2}.
\]

Multiplying by the positive number \(u^{4}\) gives  

\[
4u^{3}+32\le 64-u^{6}\;\Longleftrightarrow\; u^{6}+4u^{3}-32\le0 .
\]

Set \(t=u^{3}>0\); then \(t^{2}+4t-32\le0\), i.e. \((t+8)(t-4)\le0\), hence \(t\le4\) and  

\[
u^{3}\le4. \tag{1}
\]

On the other hand, by AM–GM, \(a+b\ge2\sqrt{ab}\), so \(v\ge2u\).  Because \(u^{2}v=8\),

\[
8=u^{2}v\ge u^{2}\cdot2u=2u^{3}\;\Longrightarrow\; u^{3}\le4,
\]

which is exactly (1).  Thus the inequality holds.  

Equality occurs when \(a=b\) (for the AM–GM equality) and \(u^{3}=4\); then \(a=b=\sqrt[3]{4}\).

### (b)  

**1.  A first estimate.**  
For any \(b,c\ge0\) we have \((b+c)\sqrt{bc}\ge2bc\) because \(b+c\ge2\sqrt{bc}\) (AM–GM). Hence  

\[
\sqrt{bc}\ge\frac{2bc}{b+c},
\qquad\text{with equality iff }b=c.
\]

Consequently  

\[
a+\sqrt{bc}\ge a+\frac{2bc}{b+c}
      =\frac{ab+ac+2bc}{b+c},
\]

and therefore  

\[
\frac{4}{a+\sqrt{bc}}\le\frac{4(b+c)}{ab+2bc+ca}. \tag{2}
\]

Summing the three cyclic analogues we obtain  

\[
\sum_{\text{cyc}}\frac{4}{a+\sqrt{bc}}
   \le 4\sum_{\text{cyc}}\frac{b+c}{ab+2bc+ca}. \tag{3}
\]

Denote the right‑hand side of (3) by \(L\).  If we prove  

\[
L\le a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}+ab+bc+ca,
\]

the desired inequality follows.

---

**2.  A convenient substitution.**  
If one of \(a,b,c\) equals \(0\), the condition \((a+b)(b+c)(c+a)=8\) forces the other two to be positive and to satisfy, for instance, \(bc(b+c)=8\) (when \(a=0\)).  Then the left‑hand side of the required inequality becomes  

\[
\frac{4}{\sqrt{bc}}+\frac{4}{b}+\frac{4}{c},
\]

while the right‑hand side becomes \(b^{2}+c^{2}+bc\); this is exactly the inequality proved in part (a) for the pair \((b,c)\).  Hence the inequality holds in those boundary cases.  For the main proof we may therefore assume \(a,b,c>0\).

\[

**6.  When is \(F(A,B)\ge 0\)?**  
Fix \(B>0\) and view \(F\) as a quadratic in \(A\):

\[

The equation \(F(A)=0\) is equivalent to \(A^{2}-4B^{2}(4B-1)A-K=0\).  Its discriminant is  

\[
\Delta_{F}=16B^{4}(4B-1)^{2}+4K
          =4B^{2}\Bigl[\,4B^{2}(4B-1)^{2}+(1+8B)^{2}(4B+1)\Bigr]>0.

The product of the roots equals \(-K<0\); therefore one root is positive, the other negative.  The positive root is  

\[

Since the coefficient of \(A^{2}\) in \(F\) is negative, \(F(A)\ge 0\) holds precisely for \(A\) between the two roots.  Because the smaller root is negative, for \(A\ge0\) this condition is equivalent to

Hence proving \(F(A,B)\ge 0\) is the same as showing \(A\le r(B)\).

\[

**9.  Completion of the proof.**  
From the discriminant argument we have \(A\le A_{\max}\) (inequality (29)).  Together with (37) this gives \(A\le r(B)\).  By the discussion in Step 6, \(A\le r(B)\) is equivalent to \(F(A,B)\ge 0\), i.e. inequality (18).  Because (18) is exactly the cross‑multiplied form of (17), we obtain \(L\le R\) where \(R\) is the right‑hand side of (16).  Recalling that \(L\) is the upper bound for the original left‑hand side obtained in (3) and that \(R\) coincides with \(a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}+ab+bc+ca\) after the substitution, we have proved  

\[
\sum_{\text{cyc}}\frac{4}{a+\sqrt{bc}}
\;\le\; a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}+ab+bc+ca
\]

for all \(a,b,c>0\) satisfying \((a+b)(b+c)(c+a)=8\).

**10.  The case when some variable is zero.**  
If one of \(a,b,c\) equals \(0\), say \(a=0\), then the condition becomes \(b\,(b+c)\,c =8\), i.e. \(bc(b+c)=8\).  In this situation the left‑hand side of the desired inequality reduces to  

\[
\frac{4}{\sqrt{bc}}+\frac{4}{b}+\frac{4}{c},
\]

while the right‑hand side becomes \(b^{2}+c^{2}+bc\).  This is exactly the inequality proved in part (a) for the pair \((b,c)\); hence it holds.  The cases \(b=0\) or \(c=0\) are analogous.  If two variables were zero, the product \((a+b)(b+c)(c+a)\) would be \(0\), contradicting the condition.  Thus the inequality is also true when some variables vanish.

Consequently the inequality is valid for all \(a,b,c\ge0\) with \((a+b)(b+c)(c+a)=8\).  This completes the proof of part (b).
